input_text: Can’t recommend in its current state, for Vive. I have done real archery, played and enjoyed several VR archery titles. For some reason the virtual arrow is frustratingly difficult to nock, and disconnects easily as though my fingers pulled right through the string or my hand pulled away. Elven Assassin is an example where once you nock, the string position is locked to your finger until you release. Similarly, the arrow angle looks and feels more natural when it sticks out from between your fingers like a cigarette rather than in line with fingers. The virtual hands and arms are not lined up at all with actual hands, fortunately can be hidden. Suggest omitting arms or wrists. Shooting between the menu letters fails. Pressing the controller menu button does not pause or bring up a menu. The level map cuts through my body around waist level, breaking immersion. Skill tree is a bit vague and not a progressively earned achievement. Verbal combo announcements quickly become annoying and don’t appear to be optional. Not sure why an archer would ever chose to stand alone in front of a gate rather than from atop a wall. A ground perspective could be logical from behind a line of soldiers who must be protected from attackers. When shooting from down near the gate, arrows keep hitting an invisible continuation of a protruding wooden beam to the left. Releasing an arrow after slow motion effect makes my released arrow fly off to the side and miss. I suspect one hand is returning to normal time before the other during dodging movement. I have a long draw length, and although I did the draw length calibration, at full draw arrows still fly much straighter than is realistic, although I have the same issue in every archery game I’ve played so far, whereas shorter players probably experience much more drop even at their full draw length. Perhaps full draw should equal 100% power, with a power adjustment setting for arrow physics. The graphics look good from what I have seen so far, and with improvements this could be a new favourite.

input_text: I played the android version of this game. I bought it to see what it was like on PC. The good parts of the game would be - having lot of levels, different gods to choose from (about 20) and some form of strategical placement when it comes to using your spells. By that, I mean that you don't just simply spam the spells as much as you want. You have to make the humans like you by casting "good" spells in order to gain worship, which is the resource used to cast other, more offensive spells for destroying their tower. Basically, you have to find a balance between appeasing the humans and pissing them off by destroying their tower. It's an interesting combination which makes it unique and offers some depth in the otherwise very standard affair of stopping bad guys from getting from one end to the other. Now for the bad. The game is an android port. It certainly looks like one and plays like one. The menus on 1920x1080 look pixelated and stretched while the models and textures are pretty lackluster. It's not ugly, but it's not pretty either. The game also starts getting pretty hectic later on, where the difficulty wasn't too well thought out and instead of thinking about enemy unit combinations and synergy, they basically throw in as many of the big units as possible to give some semblance of difficulty. After a while, the game also starts to feel like a grind, but what do you expect from a tower defence game? Problems aside, this game is pretty good for how much it costs, especially with the sale. It's a solid defence game with some nice depth to keep you interested. It's going to feel like a grind at times but if you don't mind it too much, the game is pretty fun.

input_text: This game is bloated, bland, boring and engineered to artificially keep you playing. The whole game’s progression is based on RPG-like luck-based system that is designed to you keep you playing. Even the menus are made such that you have hold a button to make your selection and there are slow animations that slow down you momentum through the game. Cars are expensive and the levelling system is based on “Popularity”, so obviously they made them a long grind. You don’t just get better quality parts because you raced well, you need to grind to level up your Icon levels, that give you points to slowly increase aspects of your performance to give you the best performance, including getting better parts for the car’s performance. And of course, there are rarities for car-parts. There are 4 main disciplines and each has several categories of events, with each event having 3 difficulties. You are forced to play the events from Easy to Difficult even if you meet the recommended performance level. The number of events per category range from 15 to 50, so you’re gonna be playing this pathetic game for a while if you wanna complete just the events in the easy difficulty. And the oblivious RPG nerds think this is the best progression in the world that is worth their time, because they have nothing better to do in their lives. Aside from this blatant attempt to artificially increase play-time, this game is riddled with technical and quality-of-life issues. It’s locked to 60 FPS, your preferred camera-view isn’t saved, pause menu has a slow animation of appearing/disappearing yet your car is moving before it completely shows/removes the menu, exiting the game is in a completely different menu, and it’s ALWAYS ONLINE!!! It’s been multiple months since they announced that they’ll make an offline version, but it’s still not here as of 10-Aug-2025. And don’t even get me started about the tone of the game. It’s the typical hApPy, qUiRkY, rAcInG fEsTiVaL with shallow characters with awful or annoying lines and typical dissociation of their lines from what you’re doing in the game. They talk about risks of falling off into the ocean, dying in an accident, putting others in danger, etc yet there’s nothing like that happening in the game. I bought this game for the promise of offline mode and cheap $1 price they did, and I regret it. $1 is the price of one person’s lunch for a day in my country, yet starving is a more fulfilling experience than playing this game. Summary of Major Issues – The level-based performance and affix system are acquired based on random chance. This system is leaning heavily towards luck rather than a player’s skill and becomes annoying over a long time, especially when you’re trying to get the best cars and parts possible. – A lot of menu options for exiting or backing out requires you to hold down the button. – Annoyingly cheerful, happy and “positive” vibes from the event topics, characters and atmosphere. o Street Racing rival keeps saying stuff like “can’t wait to see you get wrecked”, “streets are in our blood, so it doesn’t matter if my blood is on the streets”, yet nothing like that happens or has happened for the tediously long playtime that I endured through this game. § It’s not even possible to get wrecked because you can’t get wrecked. § Latrell warns about falling off the ship when drifting but all the ship sections are bordered with solid walls, so you can’t fall. o There’s an accident in the story and someone gets hurt. So you’re tasked to take him to the hospital fast but carefully while happy upbeat songs play. It doesn’t matter if you’re slow or crash your car, there’s no consequences. Being slow only shows you a “you failed” screen and there’s no dialogue from the characters about the wellbeing of the hurt person. – Summit is an event with the biggest rewards, where you complete a race/skill and you’re given scores based on how well you did. The meter shows 100k as the range, but there’s no clear indication on how the scores are calculated. You could be the first in a race by a mile and still not get 50k. – Multiple Quality of Life issues o Locked to 60 FPS. o Camera preference doesn’t stay saved. If you like the far chase cam for your cars, you will have to set it every time you launch the game. o Can’t edit downloaded liveries that are made by other people. You’re out of luck if you love how someone made black stripe pattern on a white car but you have a black car and you want white stripes. You gotta make that yourself. o If you’d like to not have the camera rotate when the plane rotates, you have to select the far chase cam. It doesn’t have a separate setting. – Heavily biased towards ground vehicles. If you got the game thinking of racing boats and planes, you’ll have very limited set of events and activities that you can do. – Scoring in drifting is either not clear or heavily biased towards chaining long drifts. Drifting smoothly through a corner carries less weight in scoring over chaining multiple smooth drifts. So if you’re having issues with a corner, your whole event’s score is vastly affected.

The BR 204 is awesome, Rivet Games did a phenomenal job with the model and the mechanics of the locomotive. They really did a great job here. The issue is that there are roughly only 5 hours of playable content before having to start replaying the same scenarios and timetable operations, this wouldn't be an issue if there were a free play mode or mission maker editor. It's disappointing to have such a great locomotive suck to a small portion of the Main Spessart Bahn. input_text: "Fill and Cross World Contest" is a basic Nonogram game... for those who never played one, it's a kind of grid-deduction-puzzle game, not unlike Minecraft or Sudoku. You're given a grid and a number of numerical clues. You must deduce where the safe places to click are. In a Nonogram, the correct clicks will reveal a small, obviously low resolution image or pattern. Yay, what fun. This is why top of the line gaming PCs costs thousands of dollars, right? The developer, Creobit, has copy + pasted this game an insane FOURTY ONE TIMES... why cash in on one asset if you can cash in on multiple copies of the same game? Asset flipping begins at home! Here's a list of the asset flips of this game that the Russian "developer" is polluting Steam with: Asian Riddles 1, 2, 3 + 4 Christmas Griddlers Christmas Griddlers Journey to Santa Detective Riddles - Sherlock's Heritage 1 + 2 Easter Riddles Egypt Picross Pharaohs Riddles Fill And Cross Christmas Riddles Fill and Cross Magic Journey Fill and Cross Pirate Riddles 1, 2 + 3 Fill and Cross Royal Riddles Fill and Cross Trick or Treat 1, 2 + 3 Fill and Cross World Contest Griddlers Beach Season Griddlers Legend Of The Pirates Griddlers TED and PET 1 + 2 (this game) Griddlers Victorian Picnic Halloween Patchwork Trick or Treat Halloween Riddles Mysterious Griddlers Magic Griddlers 1 + 2 Olympus Griddlers Picross Beach Paradise Picross Bonbon - Nonogram Picross Fairytale - nonogram: Red Riding Hood secret Picross Fairytale: Legend of the Mermaid Picross Hansel and Gretel - Nonograms Riddle of the mask Royal Riddles Santa's Toy Factory Nonograms Thanksgiving Day Griddlers Valentine's Day Griddlers 1 + 2 These are all reskins of exactly the same game! From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard. There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings. There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. The game features extremely lazy, minimalist "art", of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps. Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing. The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with crappy "wings" to pad out the space). It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming. The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff. The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction. You'll get none of that here. This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores. It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for. Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all). Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities. It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers. We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps. These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game. The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it. At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players. This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it. Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected. "Fill and Cross World Contest" has the gamer gouging price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product. For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect 2", "Euro Truck Simulator 2" or "Civilization VI". It's impossible to recommend this shovelware when there's so many better options on Steam.

input_text: 1000 hours + Ubisoft 135 hours Steam Brilliant and believable storyline. Incredible when you consider it's written pre-Covid. Scenery is amazing with immense attention to detail. Every weapon is viable; just dependent on how you like to operate. There are no better gear sets or weapons to seek after - only that which suits your approach to each mission. Even if you only played the game once through, you will never forget your experience. Although it can be multilayer, I've played and completed everything solo. I've only teamed up to help other players. Anyone claiming it to be 'dead' are those who are reliant on other players. I find that upgrading gear and weapons through natural gameplay overcomes most obstacles. Above all, experience is key. If you run around on the hardest setting a couple of hours after installing, desperately trying to increase your level super-fast, expect to get pulverised. If you call for help on those settings, and someone comes and bails you out, you get your levels and reach end game, you'll still be a noob. Experience is key. The story is everything so enjoy the journey, don't hurtle towards a predisposed destination.

I think that one of the reasons I was compelled to purchase the game was because I am very into anything astronomy. I think that this game stimulated that passion in a Sci-Fi sort of way. It isn't realistic game and it obviously isn't meant to be but that is what makes it so enjoyable. I highly reccomend this game to just about everyone, especially if you enjoy fast paced Dodge' Em Up games although I'm not a huge Dodge Em' Up guy but I think this game is spectacular. There is one and only one negative thing I have to say about this game, and that is the shortness. but other than that its amazing Once again I recommend this game to anyone, Its reasonably priced and is so much fun. input_text: I was surprised to see no reviews for this game. I am not finished by a long shot but I thought an encouraging review might help to get other people to try it. I haven't even found any bugs. It's actually a lot different than most RPG games. You go to different areas to finish the main and side quests instead of other towns. You have to either make your own potions and weapons and armor or you can buy them by going back to your own town. There are a lot of crystals to help you along in your game or to heal you. It has a good crafting system though I am never quite certain which weapon or armor a character in a game will require so I plod along. The first area of the game, you play your character alone. You do pick up another in the desert area. I'm now 19 hours in and still only in the desert. It's going to be a long game but that's ok by me. I have had to grind a lot to get the supplies I need to survive. The story is pretty good but don't expect long conversations. You get quests from people who live in your town and you farm resources laying on the ground or by defeating monsters. There is a map that stays on in the top left-hand corner that helps some to show you where you are and where an exit is. Plus, the price is right. I recommend it.

input_text: PSX inspired survival horror game with a story focused on introspection and trauma. Has a mix of Resident Evil style inventory management, Silent Hill like atmosphere, and combat reminiscent of the Fatal Frame series. If you're a fan of this era of survival horror games there's a lot to like here; it even features optional tank controls which I used through my first play-through and felt perfect. The game is ultimately more about puzzle solving and telling a story than having a deep combat system. The protagonist uses a film camera to battle enemies just like the Fatal Frame series but doesn't bring over any of that series deeper or interesting mechanics along with it. You won't be taking photos of areas to piece together clues for the ongoing story, or charging up attacks by tracking enemies and snapping shots just before enemies attack which felt like a bit of a missed opportunity. While a bit on the shorter side, I estimate around 6-9 hours on your first play, it does have multiple endings which encourages multiple runs. Recommended if you're a fan of the genre and aesthetic. Looking forward to what else this team comes out with.

input_text: This wasn't just minimal -- it was completely bare. What you see in the screenshots is essentially the entire game. While there are multiple stages (~10?), all that differs between them is the path. No new towers, no new enemies, no change in strategy -- you just plop towers down whenever you have enough money. There's never any danger of losing unless a) you didn't realize a new stage started while you were looking away, or b) your OCD kicks in and you spend too much time lining up your towers or finding the precise spot that another tower will fit. There's never any need to buy anything other than the $200 towers -- although I honestly couldn't tell whether the more expensive towers were more powerful than the cheaper ones. I like simple games, but this was more like a test project that could have used a couple of additional features. Although I bought it because it reminded me of something I might have played on the Macintosh in the 90s, many of those games admittedly had more to do. To the dev: Although I can't recommend this game, I'd be really interested in buying the sequel one day if you add more to it (strength/speed upgrades, clearer distinction between towers, better towers costing a bit more so you have to work toward them, banks or some other method for acquiring money in a different way, etc.)

input_text: Malt has very strong stats, but suffers from a lot of the same gameplay issues that can make Islay miserable to play. Malt's only way to challenge opponents requires trap cards or Gentleman's Battle. Traps are notoriously inconsistent unless you can blanket the board in them, and Gentleman's Battle is situational at best. This inability to pick your fights can make it feel like you have very little agency over how the game unfolds. That being said, the ability to turn any battle card into Assault+ is a new and interesting concept to brew with. I think clever trap placement and use of his hyper have a lot of potential in the right hands. Brewer's buzz aside, my initial impression is that he feels like a less effective version of Islay that trades precision and consistency for more opportunities to get wins. Mescal on the other hand is a much more straight-forward character with an interesting quirk. Whenever she is challenged in the field, there is a 50% chance that her opponent won't even get to fight her, battling a Pirate Crew Member instead. Thanks to her defensive stats, her pirate body guards, and the threat of Little Magnum retaliation, she can be very tough to take down. However, persistent opponents can beat their way through her defenses for some easy wins and a shot at KOing Mescal herself. If you want to try another complex defensive character Chris may float your boat. I have a hard time recommending this pack if you are only looking to grab a few, but it's definitely worth picking up at some point.

input_text: Let's start with a quick Pros and Cons list and then I'll add some depth to the review. Pros + Engaging Story + Emergent Story + Unexpected Variant Endings + Quality ambient music throughout + Best ending saved 'til last (MUST complete other endings to unlock) + No Nudity, No Sex scenes (except passionate kissing), No language, No Dating + None of the other immature 'mature' content that some authors resort to in order to increase interest in their story. Cons - Translation to English is not always strong - Fairly basic images - Images don't always show the story as written - First few endings seem arbitrary - Long periods of reading with very few choices - Dialogue lacks depth at times More Detail Starting off I was quite disappointed in this game. It calls itself a visual novel, but very little variety in the very basic visuals left me feeling that I'd wasted my money on this game (and the game is FREE). The early story feels very contrived and very predictable, in pretty much the same way as the back story of almost any cheap RPG does. I mean, seriously, three teenage boys going to spend their Halloween night in the woods where others have disappeared on past Halloweens. You have to admit that sounds as contrived as you would ever find in any game. After my first very abritrary seeming death, the only thing that kept me hanging in there was pure stubborn-ness. The game had good reviews, so surely the other choice had to be better. Each alternate path adds to the storyline, while cleverly introducing questions about the real story that kept me unsure until the very end of the final (unlocked) ending. What appeared to be a B-grade Halloween horror story turned into a well-constructed A-grade 'not horror' story (no spoilers here). It took me three hours to read through all the possible endings. So, this game is quite playable in one evening. If you have read this far in my review, let me suggest something to you. I think the story unfolds quite well if you experience the endings in an order. Without micro-analysing the endings to come up with a specific order that you would have to write down or come back and read, here's an easy way to do it that will still work well for the story: When you a given a choice to make in the game, hit ESC and save your game on the decision screen. Always take the first option whenever given a choice. After you've seen the ending, LOAD the last choice made and take the other path (all choices are binary). This will get some of the poorer endings out of the way early, and the story will unfold interestingly later (remembering that you will need to see all the endings and if you don't read your way to each ending you will miss important plot points, even on the 'bad' endings). Graphics: 3/10 Music: 7/10 Story: 9/10 Replayability: 2/10 Overall: 8/10 This game gives a good payoff for persevering. Incidentally, this is one of very few games that I have got all the Steam Achievements for.

input_text: Agenda seems to be a good concept done too simply and perhaps a bit too costly (too us gamers that is). Agenda attempts to, or at least I believe attempts to, combine the operational aspect of simulators like Evil Genius with part of the format of Plague Inc. This concept is done somewhat well but has some flaws. 1. Known bugs. I know its 2016 (state of the industry ect.) but better QA should have been done. I know part of it may be language related BUT a lot of the UI stuff should have been ironed out. Especially how sensitive the buttons are. Click the wrong place on a button and you exit the window. Speaking of Windows this seems to be only available for Windows 64 bit systems which the Dev forgot to put down which may make some users mad. 2. Goals for Regions and methods aren't so clear from the tutorial. The whole point of the game is to keep each region's power level at or just slightly above what needs to be in order to ally. This was not made entirely clear and thus may be the point of some other reviewers' frustrations. 3. One thing that is a legitimate universal complaint is the simplicity of it. Some things such as an opposing force and region specific mechanics are things that make Plague Inc. such a good game and I would advise the Devs to take note as this seems to be a very valid concern. To that end, adding events (such as those adding to or decreasing exposure or influence) would also be helpful as well as notifications as to changes in each region's desire BEFORE they break off the alliance. Furthermore, some difficulty should be added to areas other than the exposure influence mechanic. 4. Considering Number 3, this game is to expensive and is liable to create some upset people who were either expecting something closer to Plague Inc., or something closer to a political simulator. I got this on Week1 Sale but it still seems a bit steep for the content. Here's to hoping for free content updates. All in all this seems like an interesting concept but feels somewhat rushed. I would recommend it for diehard fans of the Plague Inc. type game or those nostalgic for Evil Genius type action but I would WAIT for it to fall to 5.99 USD or somewheres around there before buying it. Maybe around the holidays.

input_text: I don't remember hearing about Vellum anywhere before Steam pushed it to my recommendations, citing Roboquest as a similar title. It's a highly-competently-designed third-person roguelite shooter with a surprising amount of quality of life features and little cosmetic flourishes, some you might not even find in other quality examples of roguelite shooters. It's got up to four player coop, which you won't find in Roboquest (limited to 2 player) or Ziggurat 2, Immortal Redneck or Battle Shapers (No coop whatsoever). It's got the ability to reconnect to a multiplayer run in progress if you get dropped, which I haven't seen in ANY coop roguelites. Vellum casts the players as wizards of pen and ink, the Scribes of an endless magical library, whose tomes are gateways to worlds of fiction brought to life, but are threatened by dark creatures known as the Torn. The tomes kept in this libary act as the various rogue runs, each with unique gameplay mutators. A choice of ink color acts as your character class, providing passive abilities and modifiers to your choice of primary and secondary spells- one generates mana, and the other consumes it. Combat is of the type of rogue that I prefer, where it is balanced around your character frequently taking damage and offering various means to mitigate this- regenerating shields, stacks of damage resistance called "Varnish", the red ink class's lifesteal mechanic, etc. The library itself acts as a playable hub area in the vein of the Space Rig in Deep Rock Galactic or the Basecamp in Roboquest. Here you can find stations to change your equipped ink color or spells, and upgrade your "ink level", unlocking new passive buffs and perks, called "inscriptions." Customizing the appearance of your Scribe is also possible, with different helmets, robes, spellbooks and back accessories. Completing new tomes for the first time unlocks various features and interactables around the library, such as target dummies to gauge your damage output. There's even a nook set aside for each player to customize with decorations like furniture, paintings and the like. The commitment to the literary theme runs deep, with most mechanics, enemies and other elements having some kind of literary term to denote them- Enemy groups include Splices, Tangents and Ravings, the requisite roguelike perks are called "Pages", The yellow ink class has a critical hit mechanic referred to as "Flourish", the blue ink class has damage-over-time effects referred to as "Blot", you can get a bonus for using a specific spell and/or playing a specific tome called "Suggested Reading," and so on. These terms are almost always explained adequately and an in-game help text is available for, *ahem*, further reading. Additional mutators, called "Bindings", can be selected before a run, offering increased combat difficulty but commeasurately increased rewards of Quillmarks and Guild coins. The former is used for purchasing new spells, inks and upgrades, while the latter is for cosmetic purchases such as helmets, robes and furnishings for your nook. There are of course, no microtransactions, but who would put those in a roguelite? Uniquely, Vellum also offers endgame raid dungeons in the various Torn realms, which as of this writing I have only scratched the surface of. Much like an actual MMO raid, they appear to require a degree of team coordination much higher then the more casual tome runs. Vellum is stylish and fun to play and I highly recommend it to any fans of shooters or action roguelites.

input_text: This is a nice, casual game. The game methodology is fairly straightforward. They mix up hexagonal, colored wheels, and then you put them back in order. The hexes are in color (there is a colorblind option as well that includes patterns on the hexes) and the hub of each of the wheels tells you what hex colors go there. There are also mixed colors (yellow and red = orange; blue and yellow = green; red and blue = purple). The mixed colored hexes are, as you’ve probably figured out, for where the wheels overlap. The first two puzzle rounds show you how you will solve the remainder of the puzzles, and then you go through four grades of 12 puzzles. PRO: Very easy to learn, very relaxing and enjoyable. Good graphic representation. CON: No additional downloadable puzzles. Once you’ve gone through the 48 puzzles you can go into the options menu reset so that you can run through them again, but there is not a more difficult level to put to the puzzles. I would have loved to see more combinations. Worth the money? I would say a bit high, but I would like the programmers to give me more content so I would say it is fair enough. Would I pick it up on a Steam sale? In a heartbeat!!

input_text: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart was a new but very exciting experience for me! It was not just my first Ratchet & Clank game but also my first third-person shooter, and because of that, I did not expect to enjoy this game anywhere as much as I did! This expectation was due to the fact that I am really not good at combat in video games as a whole and I thought this would prevent me from enjoying this game, however, R&C:RA’s great difficulty options, as well as the game not being condescending about said lower difficulties, allowed me to enjoy the game at one of the lower difficulties. I personally found every aspect of this game to just be plain fun! From the gameplay, including the game mechanics, to all the collectables (my favourite video game genre is collect-a-thon platformers after all!), to the animation (so pretty and detailed!), to the writing (I laughed out loud multiple times while playing) to even the character designs (was partial to the robots as I really enjoy robots in animated media, but I think all the character designs are interesting). If like me, you have never played a Ratchet & Clank game (or a third-person shooter for that matter) then in my personal opinion I think this game is a very good place to start. Highly recommend. 10/10

input_text: It's more of Paladins VR than Overwatch VR: laggy mess with barely functional matchmaking but incredibly fun to play. Larcenauts succeeds at being a hero shooter: every class is unique and feels overpowered in its own way. Current roster has 9 heroes including archer and melee brawler. The balance is not perfect, but it's a work in progress. The gameplay is fast paced constant action: grappling points and class abilities provide fast movement while objectives discourage sitting in one place for too long. However infrequent server side lags can destroy all the fun: they range from small delays and desync to huge lag spikes that render a game unplayable for up to a minute. Shooting feels arcadey but enjoyable and there a lot of accessibility settings. I especially appreciate optional button press reloading, since Reverb G2 controllers are horrible for manual reloading. Player base is not too big for a cross-platfrom game: full 6v6 matches are only possible during peak hours. The rest of the time it will be about 3-8 players in a session with empty slots filled with bots. And AI is terrible: they can barely walk without getting stuck all the time. With small play base come issues with matchmaking: in every match experienced players will be mixed with newbies making new player experience particularly painful at times. And to add insult to injury Larcenauts matchmaking can't even distribute human players between teams equally. There are a lot of 2v4, 3v5, etc and the system doesn't bother to change team distribution between matches most of the time.

input_text: I umm'd and ahh'd as to whether to review this as recommended or not for a couple of weeks after completing. I ultimately erred on the side of recommending, as the game does deserve more attention than I feel it's gotten, but the recommendation is almost conditional on doing the YOLO (which has it's own drawbacks beyond just being another stupid platformer YOLO). Further detail below. For a casual player, the experience is short-lived. You get to the end, you get your food of choice, and you're done. This takes under 2 hours for a first play through. The additional modes do little to liven the game up, adding a new gimmick that changes how the game is played in some way that ultimately just gives the same experience with a slightly different shade of paint over the top. If your goal is to 'just get to the end', I'd recommend against the game. Where the game shines though is in figuring out cycles, figuring out approaches to make consistent that which seems like some haphazard BS the first play time through. This outcome is only achieved through the YOLO (endurance mode), assuming you don't trivialise the exercise through the use of accessibility options. I love that accessibility options are there enabling everyone to play how they feel best suits their needs, but for me, they took away from the one element of the game that made it worthwhile. I ultimately came back to the game to beat it without just the intent of ticking off 'another steam hundo'. When viewed with the lens of "I need to not die" (rather than just getting to the end), the sections are varied, the hazards are interesting, and the platforming is... well... inconsistent. Unfortunately whilst the 'levels' are interesting, the game decides it doesn't want to behave consistently. Some plays through a full jump won't clear 2x blocks, sometimes you'll get stuck in a corner, and other times you'll get pushed back by an invisible wall (that for some reason never happened in the 10hrs you'd played previously?). I've not been so frustrated with a game before due to the game itself, rather than something attributed to my own skills. So with all these caveats.... The game is flawed, the non-YOLO challenge is limited, the price is high for the content and design compared to other games in the genre... but it's a good game. A bit unpolished, a bit janky, a bit unfulfilling as a casual player.. but at the heart of it, it's a good game.

input_text: Entomophobia Entomophobia is a bug-slaying bullet-heaven where you collect a variety of unique weapons and upgrades unlike anything I have seen in a bullet-heaven so far. It currently has a few issues but it is early-access so they may be addressed by full release, it is also fairly easy once you know what upgrades to take and I found myself afking to farm the 1,000,000 kills achievement. Gameplay There are 8 characters in this game each with different stats, starting weapons and abilities, you also get a choice of gun to take with you, of which there are 5. Characters and guns can be unlocked by either completing achievements or buying them with meta-currency. There are a tonne of weapons in this game and they all act and are visually unique to anything I have seen in other bullet-heavens, how many games can you slay enemies with cornflakes, waffles and lemons while using a sniper rifle? You can take up to 5 weapons and passives total, as well as a stackable augment at every level. There's currently no way to tell when a weapon is max and there are no rerolls or banishes to help you get what you want. There are 3 maps in the game that all play basically the same as one another, the only real difference being slightly less space to move around, which is only more difficult for the first few minutes of each run. Enemies come in the same waves at the same time in each run, with each run lasting 20 minutes. Most enemies play the same but a few will back away from you while shooting projectiles and bosses come every 4 minutes or so dropping you extra upgrades. You get Shells while you play which can be spent on new characters, weapons and meta-upgrades, there are only 5 meta-upgrades that are very passive, by the time I had killed 1,000,000 bugs for the achievement I had an extra 22,000 shells that I couldn't spend on everything. There needs to be another sink to spend these on, preferably more combat upgrades. The game in it's current state is too easy, it becomes trivial after about 5 minutes if you know what upgrades to pick, I would personally like some sort of difficulty modifiers similar to 20 Minutes Till Dawn's Darkness levels that allow for a bit more of a challenge. Achievements (18/18) 95% of your time with the achievements in this game will be spent farming the 1 million bug kills, it helps to play on the River map as enemies are pushed from outside the map quite close to you and you can average around 25,000 kills per run, It took me a total of 30 hours to grind both kills and deaths. Music/sound There are a few different songs in the game that fit well, but they get repetitive after a while. Settings/Accessibility/Misc No rebindable controls. Auto-aim available. In-game achievement menu to see progress. Enemy outlines, projectile enemies are visually distinct. Settings to change the overlay colour of character, enemies, background and dangerous objects (but you can't scroll down far enough to change the dangerous objects one), these could be useful for people with colour-blindness. TL;DR Bug-slaying bullet-heaven where you collect a variety of unique weapons and upgrades. Needs more difficulty options. 3 maps that play very samey, 8 characters, 5 guns, tonnes of weapons. No rerolls/banishes. A few meta-upgrades. Very grindy achievements. Check out my Curator page

input_text: Strange Horticulture is an exquisitely crafted puzzle and exploration game that invites players into a world where botany meets mystery and folklore. Developed with an evident passion for plants and storytelling, the game offers a deeply atmospheric experience centered around running a curious herb shop in a remote and eerie village. From the moment you step into the shoes of the shopkeeper, Strange Horticulture weaves together the delicate art of plant identification with a compelling narrative that unfolds through cryptic requests, ancient secrets, and supernatural undertones. For players who enjoy slow-burning mysteries, detailed research mechanics, and atmospheric world-building, this game offers a unique and memorable adventure. At its heart, Strange Horticulture tasks players with running an old plant shop where villagers come seeking rare and sometimes bizarre herbs for their ailments or needs. The gameplay revolves around careful observation and deduction: you must examine the physical descriptions and symptoms provided by customers, then match these clues to an ever-growing compendium of plants. This process is intellectually engaging, requiring players to study botanical illustrations, cross-reference characteristics, and make informed decisions under subtle time pressure. Unlike many traditional puzzle games, Strange Horticulture rewards patience and curiosity, allowing you to gradually build knowledge rather than rush through challenges. One of the standout features of the game is its beautifully detailed plant database, which functions as both a tool and a narrative device. Each plant entry is meticulously designed, featuring hand-drawn artwork, botanical descriptions, historical uses, and notes on folklore and mythology. This encyclopedic approach immerses players in a rich world where plants carry meaning beyond their physical properties—some hold mystical powers, others are tied to local legends, and many possess symbolic weight in the unfolding story. The research element feels authentic and satisfying, giving the player a genuine sense of discovery akin to being a scholar or apothecary. The narrative in Strange Horticulture is subtle and layered, revealed gradually through the interactions with villagers, hidden notes, and the enigmatic mysteries surrounding the shop and its surroundings. The game cleverly intertwines folklore and horror, creating an unsettling atmosphere that lingers beneath the surface of its pastoral setting. Each customer’s request and story peel back another layer of the village’s secrets, encouraging players to pay close attention to dialogue and environmental cues. The story doesn’t rely on bombastic twists but rather builds tension through implication and the eerie connections between people and plants, making for an immersive and thought-provoking experience. Visually, the game is a triumph of minimalist design paired with intricate detail. The art style employs muted, earthy tones and finely drawn illustrations that evoke old botanical manuscripts and Victorian-era herbals. This aesthetic choice not only suits the game’s thematic focus but also enhances the mood of quiet mystery and antiquarian charm. The shop interface is clean and intuitive, allowing easy access to plant specimens, notes, and customer requests without overwhelming the player. Subtle animations and environmental details, such as rustling leaves or flickering candlelight, contribute to the ambiance without distracting from the core gameplay. Sound design plays a crucial role in building Strange Horticulture’s immersive atmosphere. The soundtrack consists of gentle, ambient melodies interspersed with natural sounds like wind, birdsong, and distant footsteps, all combining to create a serene yet slightly unsettling backdrop. Audio cues guide players through interactions and heighten moments of revelation or tension. The voice acting, while sparing, is well-executed, lending authenticity to the villagers’ varied personalities and enhancing the narrative depth. While Strange Horticulture excels in atmosphere and intellectual challenge, it may not appeal to all players due to its deliberately slow pace and cerebral focus. The absence of traditional action or urgent gameplay means the experience is more meditative than adrenaline-fueled. Some players might find the reliance on textual clues and botanical details a bit daunting or niche, requiring careful reading and note-taking to progress effectively. Additionally, the game’s open-ended puzzle design can sometimes lead to trial and error, especially for those unfamiliar with botanical terminology, which might disrupt the otherwise smooth flow. Technically, the game is well-optimized and runs smoothly across a variety of hardware. The interface is responsive, and the game’s minimalistic design ensures quick loading times and stable performance. The developers have also included accessibility options such as adjustable text sizes and colorblind modes, demonstrating thoughtful attention to player needs and comfort. In conclusion, Strange Horticulture is a beautifully realized and intellectually stimulating puzzle game that offers a rare blend of botanical scholarship, atmospheric storytelling, and quiet mystery. Its carefully crafted mechanics, evocative art, and immersive sound design combine to create a game that feels both scholarly and hauntingly poetic. While its slow pace and niche subject matter might limit its appeal to more casual or action-oriented players, those who appreciate thoughtful exploration and narrative depth will find Strange Horticulture to be a richly rewarding and unforgettable experience. It stands as a testament to how games can educate and intrigue simultaneously, cultivating a deep appreciation for the natural world and the mysteries hidden within it. Rating: 9/10

input_text: When I first saw COATED in the Upcoming section, it looked interesting enough to bookmark for further examination upon release. I'm grown hesitant to actually buy day-of-release games, expecially if no discount is offered. But when I saw the following message on the Store Page, the decision was made: "If you got a good experience, don't forget to mention that "Only" if you've a free moment. But in case you got a bad experience, then you "MUST" speak about it, that way you'll get better games next time." This degree of commitment made the purchase decision easy. And the first few minutes of play indicates that this may just turn out to be a very pleasant game, at a fair price (even without discount.) One thing I've learned is that the most important aspect of any new game is a concerned DEV. I wonder, however, if I'll be the only player to accidentally loose all my save data by simply attempting to exit the OPTIONS screen. I'm not sure that gameplay should be a component of the setup menus. For small children, or their beginner parents wanting to bond, this sort of rage-inducing feature might be a bad idea. If Blind Color is the same as Color Blind, having 2 levels to select for accessibility is a wonderfully kind, as well as marketable, feature. Though COATED is advertised as playable by children, don't be misled. This game is challenging enough to be interesting to gamers of any age or skill level. (I hope to update this review soon.) Thank you.

input_text: Fun mix of typing with horror, though it desperately needs a brightness slider. Try the demo to check if you can actually see anything first. I got this on offer through the Bloody Keys bundle, since I already had Blood Typers . I like typing, and typing games, but usually have a very low tolerance for genuinely scary horror. I can handle campy over the top stuff like Blood Typers and the Resident Evil games, but have never been able to get far in games like Amnesia and Phasmophobia . I have gotten all the way through to the first possible ending in Dead Letter Dept , so I think it's safe to say that it's on the lower end of scariness, though there are some slight jump-scares with static and visual effects on the screen. So far none of them have come with a loud noise though, which is usually the bigger problem. I did resort to walking backwards or while facing the floor near the end of the game though, so there might be things I deliberately missed. It's very fun and effective as a typing game, with an accessibility option to turn off cursive writing and an auto-suggest program to make sure you've typed a real address. Expect to have a lower WPM than you would normally manage though. Even if you're fearless, you're probably going to want to stop to read and process some of the things you're typing up. My main complaint is that it needs a brightness slider. I had to turn my monitor's brightness up from 20 to 100 to see anything, when the 20 setting has been perfect for every other game I play and video I watch.

input_text: Reviews for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing Overall Rating: 5/10 Gameplay Rating: 4/10 Accessibility Rating: 10/10 Overall rating is a combination of the gameplay (mechanics and story) and accessibility (how the game includes deaf/hoh gamers). General Gameplay Dysfunctional Systems is a graphic novel game that tells its story and involves the gamer in a story that plays out via text and images. You are Winter Harrison, a 14-year-old girl from a utopian world who serves as an interplanar mediator. She finds herself in Sule, a world entering into conflict that she and her mentor, Cyrus, must help resolve. If you're new to graphic novel games, the pacing is slow and story-driven. As these games go, Dysfunctional Systems' episode 1 is a short, simple introduction to the story that, though somewhat involving in its events, leaves the player left short-changed on any real development of character or story. Even so, if you have the money to spare on something you know is incomplete, this game is a small treat that can, in some ways, make up for its brevity. Replayability/Sequels While this episode has a promising start to something that could be interesting, it seems unclear whether or not there will be additional episodes following this one. General Accessibility Accessibility Options Options can be accessed before the game begins, allowing you control of game settings. Music and sound volume are controlled separately and can be muted altogether. The game plays out over text boxes. Text speed, textbox opacity and color, and the ability to skip text are all available options, giving gamers control over the pace of the game. Subtitles & Captions Dysfunctional Systems is captioned completely from beginning to end and the story plays out in text, which does not advance until the gamer decides to do so. Captions include the speaker's name and quotes for directly spoken text. Narrated text is provided without quotes and a name, so I assume it's the main character (Winter) thinking or addressing the gamer directly. The game's captions are very true to spoken word, so any deaf/hoh who do not frequently use English to communicate may find it tedious at times. Chatting/Communicating Dysfunctional Systems is a single player game; no communication/chatting options available. --- Visit Games Reviews for the Deaf/HoH [URL]

input_text: Prismatica is a color theory puzzle game where colors are scrambled and you have to rotate the gears to move the colored tiles around until they are in their appropriate places. This includes their combinations as well (example: If a red and a yellow gear have shared tiles, those tiles will turn orange). There are four total sections, each with a standard and challenge category of 12 puzzles (so there are a total of 48 puzzles that are the same in both standard mode and challenge mode). Standard mode gives you your first of three stars for that level, and challenge mode asks you to finish the same puzzle under a certain number of moves and under a certain amount of time to get the other two stars. I finished the game with all puzzles at three stars in about 11 hours. I definitely enjoyed my time with this game. I think it's great that there is a standard and challenge mode. A nice feature they included is that you don't have to finish both of the challenges at once to get the other two stars. You can focus on one at a time if you would prefer, because once you complete a task it gives you the star. This is much more preferable to having to be conscious of the moves you are making, while still moving as quickly as possible. When it came to the challenges, I felt there were levels that gave you plenty of time/number of moves to complete it, but there were also some others that felt like it didn't give quite enough wiggle room for mistakes. I did find, however, that after moving forward in standard mode, the challenge mode for earlier levels became easier to handle because of the extra practice I had gotten, so I recommend continuing standard or just jumping to a different challenge level if you are having trouble. The game settings are pretty simple, but this isn't really an issue because of the minimalist nature of the game. There is a button to toggle music on and off and another button to toggle sound effects on and off. There is also a colorblind mode that puts symbols over the colors for clearer matching. I ended up muting sound effects because they became a bit irritating to listen to. I kept the music on because it had enough variation and I enjoyed its upbeat nature. The fanfare that comes with completing a level filled me with so much joy and satisfaction. It made working through the puzzles very rewarding. I definitely recommend this game to those who are looking for a short but fun experience that exercises your brain. I felt myself starting to understand the required rotations necessary to move the tiles where I wanted to (In that respect I very much see how the Rubik's Cube inspired them), and at the end of each level I felt accomplished and pleased. Some may feel that the price is a little high with the amount of hours played, so if that's the case go ahead and get it on a sale, but I personally enjoyed the whole experience enough to say it's worth the full price.

input_text: I always enjoyed it for about 30 minutes per sitting. Any duration after that got repetitive and often annoying, despite how great the presentation was. Don't pay full price. This, the melee attack, and dash (if it worked on anything other than flat terrain) should have given some kind of buff or health/armor regen if used successfully. input_text: First Try on Top Hat The Video can be found here: [URL] Before recording and writing this review, I have played the game until Level 3-3 on normal mode, which took me about 30 minutes. First off, the options menu is relatively simplistic. You have 3 seperate sliders for audio options. Apart from that you can adjust the screen size(which I would not consider resolution options). Last, but by no means least, you can rebind the controls for keyboard and controller. Going into the game, the first thing I've noticed is that the dialogue is well translated and the jokes came across fairly well. The music is also quite good, the only minor complaint I have is that the looping of the music is a bit clunky. Gameplaywise I have to say that the gunplay(if can call it that way) and the platforming feel nice. The enemy variety and enemy design is simplistic, but it does the job. The bosses so far feel relatively underwhelming(the mechanic of the first one is easy to dodge, the second one is quite tedious to fight), but it might change later on. One thing I'd like to add before coming to the conclusion is that one of the "selling ponits" of the game is "Challenging. Really". So far I have to say, the game is not that challenging. It is more the case that the game is unforgivable in terms of mistakes. Since there are no savegame slots, you will only have one savegame. Apart from your progress your current lifecount is saved as well, which can end in a mess when you are only on one life bevore hitting a checkpoint. I can imagine that it is getting frustrating when you hit harder levels(or even bossfights) with only one life left. The question I suppose is: Is the game difficult, because it's genuinely difficult, or is it because of design decisions in terms of savepoints, etc? And in the case of top hat, I say, it is "difficult" for the wrong reasons. With that out of the way we come to the tl:dr: Is the game worth it? It is not a bad game that is for sure, but as I've stated above, I went about 1/3 through the game within 30 minutes, so you can say that your average playthrough will take you somewhat around 2 hours. And apart from Achievments and a higher difficulty levels there is not much replayability available. With that said, I'd say it's a definite buy at a sale, but if you are desperate for a nice action plattformer, you might consider buying this game even on full price.

input_text: It was an ok game, but very easy while also frustrating. There is no way to skip the tutorial, and even after that the game insists on holding your hand whether you want to or not. Puzzles are extremely easy throughout. HOS are ok, generally well translated, but the ones that are not are extremely confusing. Also, the misclick penalty seems to just be about number of misclicks in a row, with no timer involved. Towards the end of the game, it becomes frustratingly hard for all the wrong reasons. There are hints, but only text ones, and no map indications, so you spend most of your time running around trying to find a person with something new to say, but in most cases, which of the HOS's has reactivated. And for my taste, there were way to many of those, especially compared to the few puzzles. The hints might tell you what to do to meet your objectives, but they tended to point to the wrong ones, while also spoiling the already too easy puzzles. Two of the last few puzzles even had built in backtracking. The story is the usual kind for this kind of game, when it is there at all, but I wasn't expecting much from it. It has an ok base, honestly, but some very bad design choices made it mainly frustrating. The short bit between they stopped telling you what to do before you just had to guess where to go was ok? I honestly can't recommend it, even on sale. Hopefully the devs learn from the experience and get better with time.

input_text: The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is a thoughtful and endearing point-and-click adventure that builds on the quirky charm of its predecessor, deepening the narrative and expanding the strange, whimsical world of Asposia. Developed by Studio Fizbin and published by Headup Games, the game offers a blend of clever puzzles, heartfelt storytelling, and richly imaginative world-building that appeals to fans of both classic adventure titles and modern narrative-driven games. While it remains grounded in traditional point-and-click mechanics, The Last Wind Monk excels by infusing its universe with emotional depth, character growth, and a surprising layer of political and philosophical commentary. The story picks up a few years after the events of the first game, once again following Robert, the unlikely hero and flute-nose monk, who has been in hiding since the rise of a fanatical regime bent on eradicating his kind. The antagonist Emil, a populist tyrant, has spread propaganda that blames the flute-noses for Asposia’s past misfortunes. Robert must now team up with returning characters like the spirited Laura and the ever-loyal pigeon Peck to find the mythical last Wind Monk and restore peace. What begins as a whimsical journey soon reveals itself to be a surprisingly poignant tale about intolerance, identity, and the misuse of power. The themes are handled delicately, balancing humor with introspection and satire with sincerity. Visually, The Last Wind Monk is a joy to behold. The hand-drawn art style, filled with odd, soft-edged characters and surreal landscapes, creates a world that feels like a cross between a children’s storybook and a surrealist painting. The environments are packed with detail and personality, from gloomy prison cells to vast underground temples and lively cityscapes. Each area feels distinct and alive, with cleverly designed layouts that encourage exploration and interaction. The animations are smooth and expressive, lending additional character to every NPC and making even minor interactions feel rewarding. The gameplay sticks closely to the genre’s roots, emphasizing item collection, environmental interaction, and puzzle-solving. What sets it apart, however, is the variety introduced through character switching. Players can control Robert, Laura, and Peck at different points, each with their own abilities and perspectives. Peck, for example, can fly into otherwise inaccessible areas, while Laura’s no-nonsense attitude often drives narrative momentum. The puzzles themselves range from simple to delightfully convoluted, often requiring players to combine items in unconventional ways or interpret dialogue clues carefully. At times, puzzle logic may feel obtuse, but the integrated hint system ensures that players who get stuck can move forward without too much frustration. The voice acting and writing deserve particular praise. The English voice cast delivers consistently strong performances, with Robert’s earnestness, Laura’s sarcasm, and Peck’s chirps and squawks all contributing to a warm and often hilarious tone. The dialogue is witty and smart, balancing slapstick humor with deeper philosophical questions. Studio Fizbin has a gift for writing dialogue that’s playful yet meaningful, often masking social commentary beneath layers of absurdity. The localization is excellent, retaining the humor and nuance of the original German version without losing cultural relevance or tone. The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is not without flaws. Some players might find the pacing a bit slow in certain sections, especially when backtracking through areas or solving particularly complex puzzles. Additionally, while the game expands on the lore of Asposia, it relies heavily on familiarity with the first game—new players might feel slightly lost without having experienced Robert’s original journey. That said, for returning fans or those willing to dive into the world of Asposia from the start, the payoff is rich and rewarding. In conclusion, The Inner World: The Last Wind Monk is a charming and surprisingly poignant adventure that combines the classic appeal of point-and-click gameplay with modern storytelling finesse. Its unique visual style, engaging puzzles, and heartfelt narrative create an experience that’s both whimsical and reflective. It’s a game that dares to be silly while also addressing serious themes, offering a thoughtful commentary on prejudice, fear, and hope in a world that feels just fantastical enough to mirror our own. For players who appreciate narrative-driven adventures with personality, warmth, and just a touch of melancholy, this game is an easy recommendation. Rating: 8/10

input_text: Has potential but is really limited. This is one of those games if you want to call it that where you check in every once in a while and develop more conversation points with the person. The communication is okay but is too repetitive and schedule dependent to be of interest. I think one of the conversations that threw me off went something along the lines of this when I checked in after some time hoping to spawn new conversation points: Hey it's been a while since we've talked. You should ask how was your day. I'm not being pushy or anything "How was your day?" Hmm my day let me think, did anything interesting happen? No, but thanks for asking. Pros +Simple to understand +Good translation +Cute anime girl? Cons -Repetitive conversation -Relies on exact entering of key terms and questions to understand - AI understanding just falls short So if you want an ai bot for conversation you can go elsewhere. There are free bots such as cleverbot that has more foundation. This just can't stand well on it's own despite it's anime girl presentation. If it had more dialogue branches and choices than it could be a fun little simulation. I'd say pass on it though. Follow my reviews through my curator at Crim's Humble Opinion

input_text: A fantastic VN with a very high production value. Kinda blown away with the music in it, as there are several theme and ending songs with full vocals and a wide variety of music types. The story is extremely well done and unique (I have 100+ VNs and nothing even similar to this one), and the voice work is top notch. The translation is generally good. There are a number of spelling errors, but the tone and flow of the English language translation is good and sounds very natural. Overall; the localization team for English did an excellent job. My only complaint is that skipping text to complete all of the endings is very tedious, as the skipping feature is stopped every scene change, where the screen fades out and back in, or where the chapter animations are. This is a minor complaint, but it did add significant time to the acquisition of all endings. I recommend saving at every decision branch to facilitate completion of all of the endings. Also; Litona is adorable and Aco is amazing. I need an altruistic magical girl and sassy A.I. irl asap.

input_text: A cute and engaging otome game, set during a cat princess's diplomatic visit to a human kingdom in a time when there is still some contention between the two races. The story switches focus back and forth between a budding romance and the more serious sociopolitical issues faced as the princess struggles to do what is best for her people. The English translation is excellent, the characters endearing, and the humor delightful. I have played it through once so far and enjoyed it immensely. There is of course replay value as well, there being two routes you can experience (or a mix thereof). Learning that this is a stand-alone entry in a game series I expect I'll be trying more titles from this developer in future.

input_text: I love Stronghold Crusader, having played a TON of it in childhood and adulthood. As games go, it's meant a lot to me over the years. There are good things about this game, but overall, it's not worth your $25. FireFly are doing what they do, trying to grab your cash while coasting on nostalgia and dwindling goodwill. The updated artwork is more detailed, but not all of it looks better. Most of it looks great, but some of it looks very bad. Certain animations are choppy or otherwise look odd. Multiplayer seems to work fine, though there are latency issues that are unacceptable for a modern RTS of this price. I'll note that in the first co-op trail scenario, my cousin and I encountered a glitch where our troops couldn't pass through our gatehouses. How something that fundamental gets screwed up on a remaster, I don't know. Edited after playing a little more.

input_text: TL;DR: Unique multiplayer, but rough around the edges. Cheaters are everywhere, the anti-cheat is as real as winning a war against a weak neighbor country in one month, and both MMR and netcode feel like they were coded by interns on their first day. Matches are long, unbalanced, and full of quitters, which is more of a design flaw than a player issue. Single player is not worth touching. Updates arrive slowly, marketed as “meaningful,” but usually fix little while breaking something else. Buy it on sale, know exactly what hole you are jumping into, and you might have some fun. Just do not expect anything close to polished or professional. Buy it for the multiplayer only, and train yourself to turn off half your brain, since rush B is always the meta. There is no real anti-cheat, so cheaters are as common as mosquitoes in summer. It got so bad that the developers had to lock the cheater report thread on Discord because they could not keep up and it was making the game, and some regions of the world, look even worse. MMR is broken, the netcode is unreliable, and it shows. Matches can last 45 minutes or more, there is no option to forfeit, and players quit constantly. The developers keep saying they will punish quitters, but the problem is not the players, it is the design. Matchmaking is sloppy, balance is inconsistent, and the so called rock paper scissors mechanic rarely applies in practice. People are not leaving because they are bad, they are leaving because nobody wants to waste nearly an hour, including the lobby and matchmaking wait, on a match that is doomed from the start. I have played over 100 matches without quitting, the only times I disconnected were due to crashes or connection issues, which is just another headache. That being said, there is nothing else quite like it. WARNO might come close in gameplay, but its community is probably just as questionable. Single player is the comedy act nobody asked for. You cannot save mid mission, some missions take hours, and the AI is both dumb and omniscient at the same time. It feels like fighting a wallhack bot that still makes terrible decisions. Funny to watch, awful to play, and definitely not worth the effort. The game goes on sale often. I pre ordered the Vanguard Edition, refunded it on launch day, and bought the Standard Edition for 20 percent less the same day. No regrets there. When it works, which is maybe 50 to 60 percent of the time, it is genuinely fun. The rest of the time you are just spinning the wheel of crashes, ragequits, and hackers. Do I recommend it? Yes, but only on sale and only if you keep your expectations in check. Go in expecting a smooth experience and you will end up saltier than the BA mods on Discord. PS: I also wrote a guide on how to quit the game, since the quit button itself usually does not work.

input_text: The game, when first released, was an experiment for Boomzap as they wished to branch out into the Strategy genre after having made their name with Hidden Object games. This game quickly became one of my favorite indie games and is quick and easy to pick up and play, while offering quite the challenge as you move through the campaign. They also released a mobile version of the game, and buying one version (mobile or PC) gave you the other version for free, allowing you to continue through your campaign through either method. Within the past year or so, issues arose with the authentication server, which made the game impossible to play beyond a demo like mode if you installed it on a new device. The devs indicated that it would be costly, if not impossible, to fix those issues due to the backend coding that allowed them to connect mobile and PC versions. Gratefully, though, they have worked to get the PC version back up and running, though Multiplayer needed to be disabled in order to do so. I still recommend this game as it's a fun game to play. I am by no means an expert in the Strategy genre. I have played games like Civilization, Total War, Risk, Stronghold, et al. but haven't played any with the card mechanic like this that I recall, so can't make comparisons. All I can say is that I have enjoyed this game from the start, and look forward to continuing through the campaigns at my leisure, and playing those skirmishes, which I have done a lot of. The loss of multiplayer and mobile suck, but at the end of the day, despite losing money on this experiment, the devs put forth the effort to get the PC version back up and working and are to be commended for doing so.

input_text: I stopped playing about a month ago because constant leavers killed the fun for me and my friends. Today I decided to give it another shot to see if things had improved. Spoiler: they haven’t. The following is a good example of the current state and average experience with this game: I qued up for two games. First queue: two players on the enemy team disconnected during loading and never came back. We spent 45 minutes in unfun seal-clubbing because there’s still no surrender option. Second queue: waited ~7 minutes, got kicked from the queue with a connection error. Restarted the game and queued again. Then had to wait another 7 minutes. - My own account that I previously queued with then somehow ended up on the enemy team, so I basically played against myself. - My deck that picked didn’t transfer into the match (probably because I was in the lobby twice). - Enemy players were displayed as “friendly” in chat. - I couldn’t spawn units at all! - After leaving the game, I couldn’t even rejoin. - When the match ended, I still got slapped with a full -25 ELO penalty. - Potentially had to wait another 5-7 min to find the next match - i quit instead. The gameplay itself is fun when the core game functions actually work, but that’s the problem, they rarely do. Add in constant bugs (invisible units, rubber-banding, hits not registering, LOS not working), broken reporting/anticheat, and poor connection stability… and it’s pretty clear why hardly anyone is still playing this game. I can’t really comment on the single-player aspect since I only played two missions, but it still has no save function since launch. In this state this RTS is definitely not worth a hefty 50 EUR. EDIT - 29.08.2025: The latest balancing patch has made an already dominant RU faction even stronger, rendering some US deck combinations almost unusable.

input_text: Diablo 4 Beta Review Rating: 8/10 After spending several hours playing the Diablo 4 beta, I can share my thoughts on what Blizzard is preparing for the full release. Overall, the beta gave a good preview of what the game will offer, with plenty of positive aspects but also a few issues that need attention before the final launch. Positives: Environment and Graphics: There’s no denying that the world of Sanctuary looks stunning. The dark and detailed atmosphere truly immerses you in the game. The lighting, the intricate cityscapes, and the dungeons, along with how the environment interacts with weather effects, are all impressive. It’s a living, breathing world that adds another layer of immersion. Combat and Gameplay: The combat system is dynamic and very satisfying. The fluidity of animations and quick response of controls make battles visceral and engaging. I played as both the Barbarian and the Sorcerer, and both classes are a lot of fun, with distinct abilities and build possibilities that encourage experimentation. The feeling of power when wiping out hordes of enemies is something the franchise has always nailed, and it’s no different here. Progression and Customization: Character progression is one of the standout features. The skill system offers deep customization, allowing players to create unique builds. The fact that every skill has a meaningful impact on gameplay ensures that players feel a constant sense of evolution, with rewards at each new level. Open World and Multiplayer: The option to play in a shared, open world with other players is one of the most interesting innovations in Diablo 4. Dynamic events, like monster invasions and boss fights, make exploration more engaging. And of course, interacting with other players, even in a non-forced way, adds an extra layer of fun. Negatives: Server Issues (Beta): As expected, the beta wasn’t free from server issues. There were times when wait times to enter the game were long, and lag hindered the experience. While these issues are common in beta phases, they still impacted the flow of gameplay and caused some frustration. Content Repetition: Although the story hooked me, I felt that some quests and side activities started to feel repetitive after a few hours. The main story quests are interesting, but the side missions often don’t offer much variety in objectives, which can become tiring for more dedicated players. Limited Beta Content: The beta, while giving a solid idea of what to expect, also left a sense of incompleteness. Some features and areas of the game were locked, meaning we couldn't experience the game in its entirety. It left me with the feeling that the core of the game will only truly shine once the full version is released. Monetization and Microtransactions (Concerns): While the beta didn’t directly showcase this, the question of microtransactions and monetization still looms large. It wasn’t clear how Blizzard will balance this aspect, especially in a game that has the potential to be a massive hit among RPG and ARPG fans. I just hope the experience isn’t negatively impacted by excessive monetization practices. Conclusion: The Diablo 4 beta at the time in 2023 left me excited for the full release. Blizzard has nailed several aspects, like combat, character progression, and creating a dynamic open world. However, some server issues and content repetition still need to be addressed. In summary, Diablo 4 has the potential to be one of the franchise’s best titles, but a few tweaks are needed to perfect it. For long-time fans of the series, it’s definitely worth keeping an eye on the official release, and I hope Blizzard can deliver a polished, varied experience.

input_text: It’s a cute game, but I fully admit that I don’t have any strong feelings about it one way or the other. But again, for a $5 otome game, I wasn’t expecting an Idea Factory narrative. In conclusion: It’s a short game you can finish in less than a day, it has it’s cute moments, and the art is pretty, so go ahead and buy it if you like the beach and shirtless mermen. It's only $5 after all. On a side note: there was a scene near the beginning of the game that was unintentionally funny? It was a pan up of Crylis (The merman’s) sprite, and for some reason this merman sprite descending from the heavens was just the funniest thing to me. Don’t ask me why; it was late, I was kinda tired, and I have a terrible sense of humor.
