input_text: Multi-path stories sim Using various types of stat values in each story, the player can manipulate how the story goes. Ruin the character’s life or make it as best as it can be. Praises • Emma’s story path gives some insight into the type of bullsh*t women put up with in a male-dominated workplace. • Paul’s story path demonstrates how ridiculously corrupt and hypocritical politicians are. • There is a decent amount of diversity among all the characters of the game. • The game made me chuckle a couple of times. Complaints • Lots of typos. A few sections of text left untranslated from French. Some awkward translations to English. • Imbalanced elements in gameplay. • Jenny’s story path is boring. I had so little motivation to finish it because there was nothing interesting about it. It seems like it was supposed to be about bullying and dealing with college, except bullying is rare in college; that’s more of a k-12 thing. Regardless, the point of it was just so poorly-written and weak. • (Possible Bug) During Jenny’s story path, it is not even remotely obvious how you’re supposed to inform Hamim about Mika’s internship. There are no options for it anywhere, then the two friends get upset because the event never occurs. • (Bug) During Jenny’s path, it seems like there isn’t a way to stop Mika from committing the prank, even though on the branch map, it insinuates there is. • (Bug) On Jenny’s path, the revision notes do not refresh for a new playthrough, making it impossible to know how many the player actually has for that playthrough. They do not stack through playthroughs. • While Paul’s story path addresses the importance of environmentalism, it does the typical mistake of putting the responsibility mostly on general individuals rather than the billionaires whose industries are almost entirely responsible for climate change. Furthermore, the socialist politician character in his story would’ve made that point by arguing that eliminating capitalism would absolutely lead to better environmentalism and she unrealistically makes no such argument. (I am not suggesting people should stop individually doing things that help the environment. I am just pointing out that if you want to stop the planet from burning up in a few generations, the only way to do that is to stop the billionaires and their industries. There is no other way, because it is literally them killing the planet with their industries.) • (Bug) Jordan’s story path seems entirely messed up because in order for him to confess that he’s gay to people, he needs enough morale, but he never has enough for what is required and there is seemingly no way to increase the max amount of morale. It’s just 3. I can’t tell if the bug is that there are suppose to be more or that the method of increasing the max morale is not presenting itself. But yeah, it’s impossible to confess to anyone. Considering the game was released in 2021 and there are several improvements that need to be made, I can’t recommend the game. It’s a cool concept, but executed poorly. It is seemingly impossible to get a lot of the achievements.

input_text: This would be a decent short point and click adventure title were it not so… slapdash. The English translation is pretty engrish, though the voice acting isn't that bad. Some locations have two music tracks accidentally playing on top of another and the game characters have entirely different design and looks during in-game and cutscenes. (The protagonist alternates between having a black three-day stubble and a shaved face with silver moustache – and gains about 20 years of age!) Puzzles can be roughly divided into two categories – there's item-using puzzles that fit the world, and random bouts of sudoku and tic-tac-toe that seem there just for filler. And I had the tic-tac-toe glitch on me. It's just so half-hearted and I'm willing to give historical adventure titles quite a bit of leeway. I suppose the best thing about this game is that the journal in the inventory works as a walkthrough if you get stuck. (Oh yeah, I left the game on for an entire day by accident so that's why the long duration. It's not that long.)

input_text: This game is pretty good. There are a few issues that can be sorted out with some extra time, but for the most part it's enjoyable and solid. Will list pros and cons below. I will say, many people say the game is too easy, but I feel that they must have only played the first initial playthrough based on time spent and my own experience of how the difficulty definitely gets up there. Can recommend for anyone who enjoys a card drafting game, roguelike gameplay, and the like. PROS ~Polished and unique art style ~Very nice soundtrack ~Cards seem decently balanced so far ~Board game-esque exploration is visually pleasing and entertaining ~Mechanics are solid and easy to learn ~10 hours in and still finding new combos, and have only played 1/3 of the initial roster ~Interesting legacy system with currency to boost a struggling run (not microtransaction, earned in-game) CONS ~Poorly translated at times (easily patched but worth noting) ~Similar to StS, the game feels like its over right when i'm getting a good deck going. Needs longer modes. ~Some mechanics are confusing until tried. For example, keywords like "Transform" discards the card and makes a token during combat, but changes a card into something else permanently out of combat. ~Typos on certain things like "sepll" instead of "spell" (again, easily patched but worth noting) ~Asks for online server choice even though the game is entirely offline, so you must have internet to play. (Why?) All in all, with some polishing this game could be one of my go-to's. As it stands I will keep playing it for probably another 20 hours or so, unless something really keeps my attention. ~~Current Rating~~ 8/10

input_text: It's hard, it's a little sparse, and it's maybe not supported any more, but Deep In The Forest isn't bad. Graphically, it looks very polished. The art is lovely and has its own strong sense of style. But the game is made by a tiny team, so don't expect something as expansive as Slay The Spire. Instead, Deep is a relatively small-deck, combo-focused deckbuilding game. Mana accumulates rapidly, and you can mulch a card each turn to increase your mana gain, so the restriction on most of your turns is hand size. Beyond that, Slay The Spire is a pretty close comparison. You try to dps your enemies down before your turn ends and they damage you, and you have an inventory into which you can load passives to help you in fights. Unlike Slay, Deep has hard progression. Your deck and your level carry over from run to run, and I suspect you may need to grind them both to get past the first boss. This also means you can maybe accidentally build a garbage deck and have to reset your campaign, as combo synergy is *really* important in deep. Deep has an open map, and allows backtracks, but it tries to dissuade players from leveling up too much by causing all enemy damage values to go up the longer you take. This...doesn't interact perfectly with the leveling up system, but I guess it makes hard mode more exciting. I'll update this review if gameplay changes significantly as I continue, but as-is it's kind of a good time-kill. I don't feel the "just one more run" effect I get from Spire, and that's kind of a good thing. I can grind a bit, lose, and go back to what I was working on before I decided to take a break, rather than dumping a whole afternoon into a game. Edit: You have to grind for like an hour out of the gate, but after that the game gets pretty flexible and fun. There's room to explore a few different strategies, and later enemies have fairly complex behaviors (do X after you play two cards, do Y after you attack twice, do Z after you heal,) but you'll need to unlock some cards and gain a few levels to get to the good bits. If you get this, push past the three hour mark. It's much more rewarding than I expected. 2nd Edit: There are some weaknesses in the writing. Typos and strange grammar in a few places. They don't interfere with understanding the game mechanically (for the most part,) but the dialog after each boss is supposed to feel significant and dramatic, and the writing sometimes spoils that effect.

input_text: Fading Hearts is not one of those games which will really win an award for spelling, nor will its story win an Oscar by any means. Fading Hearts as a VN game is confident, but that comes with some spelling errors. So if you’re a grammar N…Z or an English teacher, it’s not advisable to pickup and play this game. It could possibly drive you insane by the spelling mistakes in this game. Also if by chance you’re picky on fictional settings and places not fitting in the logic of the real world then don’t pick this game up. But if you’re old enough to remember the ridiculous plots and plot holes of older Japanese VN games from the 80’s. Then you might have an idea what to expect as a back story plays out. In Fading Hearts Y2K led to a disaster which only affected one small nation in the whole world. That small nation is where our main catalog of characters in this game live. This leaves our main protagonist and his friends without parents because of the disaster which had befallen the small country of Sorayama. Personally, I had to stop playing for a bit because I was laughing for a while after reading it. But after getting my composure back I found out that I enjoyed Fading Hearts as a whole game. With all that said, technically the game does everything VN games have done in the past and doesn’t really break that mold. That is not really a bad thing as VN games were always about how you discovered the world around you, but also the people you interacted with. That in itself, is what Fading Hearts does right, it gives you the ability to choose how you want to pursue your relationship with those characters’. As well as how your choices will affect the final ending of the game itself. So if you’re a relaxed person whom happens not to get too stuck up on a few spelling errors and an off the wall notion of the world Ryou lives in, give this game at least a shot.

input_text: After several hours in this game, I have come mainly to one conclusion. I feel bad for the money I spent. The game is basically a mediocre shooter with mobile style controls (you autoaim nonstop with almost no control over where to aim) and there is a horrible grind to it. The graphics are servicable, the sound is servicable, nothing breathtaking. It's not technically *bad*. It just makes you wonder after paying 15 bucks what you paid for. The writing in the game contains errors after you switch to english, typos or even words leftover in french. There are no mouse controls but the game has buttons...? Why? Furthermore, the biggest challenge in the game is either being overwhelmed by enemies because you didn't grind enough to get better weapons, of which there are only 3 main weapons locked to shiptypes, minus the skills you use, OR the fact that some enemies can simply outright murder you without you having any chance to fight back. Some basic enemies can oneshot you with insanely fast missiles and they don't fire a single one, no, they fire several. Also they can and will fire from offscreen and they fly faster than anything else in this game, making dodging impossible. So you die randomly. Then you grind so you don't die. And even after that you still die. <- this is the non fun part The grind consists of running the same missions over and over again on easy mode, because there is literally no point in going for medium or hard since you get the same payout. And then you make like... in the beginning about 300 stars maybe? Middle game 700? depends where you grind and how good you are. And then you have upgrades that give you tiny advantages that cost you like 3000+ stars. Grind. Die. Repeat. Eventually you progress, which is not something you can really enjoy because all the game does is throw more enemies at you. I rarely had a moment where I can say "I got here because of skill, not luck". This is what pains me. The bossfights are decent, those are actually fun. They are not random. The bosses don't use unreasonable weapons to artificially make the game hard. The rest of the game is just a slog. For 12,49€... yeah, I should have gotten something better. The quality is not there and the game is ultimately not motivating.

input_text: The Translation's Power Level is Too Low Story If you judge the game based on the title, you're probably assuming that this is going to be similar to Final Fantasy IV. In reality, this game is an over-the-top Shonen anime power fantasy. While there is some overlap between JRPGs and the Shonen anime genre, this game has more Shonen tropes than the average JRPG. The protagonists are constantly in search of powerups to overcome the current unbeatable foe, only to overwhelm the boss once they get those powerups, and this repeats until the protagonists and enemies are god-tier. Many of the important duels and boss battles end with the main character getting knocked to low HP, only to get a scripted finishing move while spewing hammy lines, which I find oddly satisfying. If you enjoy Shonen anime, this is the game for you. If not, then I don't know what to say. For the most part, the plot is nothing too groundbreaking. You control a knight-turned-paladin who has to go around the world in order to stop a conspiracy of Extra Gems and Miasma. That said, the main characters are charming in their own ways, making the story enjoyable despite the clicheness. As for the villains, I enjoyed Red Rose, the second duel opponent, and the final chapter villain for their morally gray aspects. However, I think some major villains, such as Berienstahl and the Chapter 3 main antagonist, need more depth. That said, the plot point where we lose the first healer and the party gets framed is really contrived, since there's no effort to show fabricated evidence and therefore the healer should have no reason to believe in the party's guilt. Unfortunately, the current translation is terrible and pretty much reads like a barely edited machine translation, to the point where there are even untranslated lines. Worse yet, not everything is translated consistently, such as how the Flotsam is also called the Soaring Stone and how the dictionary uses both "Alec" and "Alex" as the name of the rival character. While the translation can be unintentionally funny at times, it can be very annoying for parts of the game where you have to make choices based on dialogue. It's a real shame, since I feel like the game would be a great Shonen power fantasy otherwise. Gameplay Yes, the Shonen tropes carry over into gameplay. The equipment system is set up so that the player can only change ornaments and skill gems while everything else is determined by the story. This allows the story to maintain relative power levels between the characters, since stats from equipment matter more than stats from leveling. Fortunately, the skill gem system is designed so that it's possible to make even low-tier characters effective as support casters for stronger characters, so it's still balanced in a way. Speaking of relative power balance, the Paladin class is designed to be overpowered, since it has very high stats and constantly learns new skills, making it a Super Swiss Army Knife. Normally, it's not good for one single character to carry all of the game's buff skills, but this is balanced by a mechanic that allows Nade to share his Paladin skills with other characters. This will make it easier to apply the Paladin's powerful buffs quicker, since the Paladin's skillset can be divided among five party members. One of my favorite features is the formation system, since it allows the player to cast an instant buff on the party and control how much enemy aggro the party members get. It reminds me of both the formation system from Nocturne: Rebirth and the Brave Order system of Trails of Cold Steel III/IV . That said, the game does throw a lot of miasma using enemies at the player in the endgame, meaning the Sword of Paladin formation ends up the only viable option for long battles. This is balanced by the Commander gem, which gives access to other formations' buffs. The game has a duel system that works similarly to Suikoden . Melee allows Nade to guard against a ranged attack before striking back, ranged attacks can safely damage a countering enemy, and counterattack allows Nade to negate a melee attack before striking back. This requires the player to memorize the enemy's dialogue to figure out which action they're going to do, though later battles also require the player to memorize facial expressions. Sadly, this system has two major pitfalls. One is that melee vs ranged still results in damage to the melee user, which is bad for the player on hard mode because they'll still take more damage to their total percentage of health than the enemy. The other flaw is that the bad translation can make it hard to discern the enemy's intention. As for the game's difficulty, I played most of the game on hard mode. It's fairly balanced, but the difficulty can fluctuate a lot due to the story-enforced power levels. Once Nade gets his Paladin abilities, he's very powerful compared to even bosses and shouldn't have much trouble at all. However, when the game forces the player to control a party of lower-tier characters, the difficulty skyrockets, though it's still possible to win all the mandatory battles with some effort. Verdict 7/10, this game is the embodiment of the meme, "I have the power of God and anime on my side!" The game has a decent story and is well-balanced for the most part. However, the translation doesn't do the game justice at all. I really hope the game will get a better retranslation in the future so that it'll be easier to appreciate its sheer Shonen anime energy.

input_text: This game is tons of fun. I don’t remember the last time a game made me laugh so much. I bought it because I wanted a classic turn-based RPG game with nice art and good story. It has all that and more. So, here are the good points. The art is great. The Celestials are the best-looking characters ever. The story is great and shines even through the bad translation. Lots of humor. The MC and other human warriors are the “brawn no brain” type and that leads to hilarious dialogues. Celestials are on a different level, they crack jokes intentionally. I loved Ishbel’s insolent sarcasm and Siegfried’s morbid jokes. Unfortunately, we only get about 40% of it, the rest is lost in the translation and the only way you could guess there was a joke is because the dialogue looks particularly awkward. Still, enough come through to make you laugh. Characters. Again, they are on two different levels. Humans are very cliché, nothing to say about them. Celestials are intriguing, they have complex past stories and relationships that the main story only hints on. Wish I could know more. Autobattler! It’s epic. It starts as a standard plot with the kids as main characters, but before you even get to the mid-game, you start recruiting the godlike Tetrarchs into your party. Next thing you know, you play with demi-god characters with abilities on par with their high stats. Yeah, I know, it’s all balanced and the enemies can thwart their efforts, but I don’t care, I just love to see Siegfrid use that insta-kill spell. Not intentionally, translation bloopers make it hilarious. So do the outrageous stats. After they reached level 25, I found myself saying “my attack stat is WHAT now?” a lot. Really, when do you see your attack going over a thousand? It gets better, you have an achievement to do 3,000 in one blow. Once you do that, there is 10,000. Then 30,000. And yes, you can do all that. I couldn’t help laughing when I did it, it’s just so unusual, yet, so appropriate for having demi-gods in your party. Well, there are cons. The translation is very uneven and seems to be done by at least two different people, if not more. The worst part is the skill descriptions. The person who translated it had no idea what increase and decrease mean. Do not trust the descriptions, just try the skill out and see what it really does. It’s simple enough to figure out. It’s easy to learn and easy to play. Some people may see it as not enough challenge. I love to tinker with the party composition and equipment, so I loved it, but that’s your primary challenge. If you are looking for something else, you may be disappointed. In conclusion, yes, do buy this.

input_text: Positives Plot: I thought the plot and premise was quite good. I don't know why but I kept thinking of a game called The Dig whilst playing this, got a similar vibe for some reason. I'll comment later on in the review how this was let down in some ways but otherwise it's one of the more interesting hidden object games on Steam. Aesthetics: Some locations look a bit too similar IMO but that doesn't stop the game looking pretty. The music was also quite atmospheric which is always nice in a HOG. The UI is okay but getting the inventory bar out of the way got a bit annoying sometimes ;) Achievements: While some might see this as a negative it was a nice break to play a HOG without any punishing achievements! Depending on the difficulty level you play through, you can also get them all in one run which may appeal to some people :) Value for money: I got just over 3 hours of play time out of this game and for once it wasn't one I'd leave running in the background while I wandered off to do something else. That was one full run through then a short play through just to get one of the achievements I'd missed, so to me this game has paid for itself in game time. There are games on Steam for more money than this that offer less content! Hints: I was getting butt mad and was going to review this game differently until I realised it was my own fault I was struggling! Use the little mobile PC in the bottom left of the screen, it contains a lot of information that will help you. I assumed it would just be like the typical HOG diary and log what you had done but it actually gives you some nice little hints ;) Puzzles: The puzzles in this game are a lot easier than other HOGs on Steam IMO but I didn't see this as a bad thing, the game more than makes up for it with the hidden object puzzles, of which there are a-plenty ;) Negatives Backpedalling: Maybe it's just me but I get bored quite quickly with hidden object games that require a lot of clicking back and forth between screens to trigger events. There isn't too much of it in this game, but there are times where you will be looking around for ages trying to figure out where to go and it's because the screen you were on ten minutes ago has an event but because you didn't go back to it immediately after leaving that screen. Cut scenes: Don't hate me but I can be super impatient, so waiting for an oiler to oil four seperate pieces of machinery really slowly just sets me off haha! I wish some of the actions and cut scenes were a bit faster, purely because I want to get back to the game. Just personal preference though ;D Text: The only thing I really disliked with any depth was the text in this game. I think the vibe the developers were going for was great, but it was ruined by multiple typos and poor translations. This isn't the only HOG on Steam to have this problem, and it doesn't make me think any less of the game but I think it's selling the game and all the hard work put into it short. TLDR: A nice take plot wise, two seperate teams were an interesting concept. Marred by some poor translations/typos and occasional backpedal frenzies but otherwise a well thought out HOG that is definitely every bit a HOG! Lots of hidden object puzzles that are challenging at times. If you're looking for a relaxed game that is easy to 100% then Mystery of a Lost Planet is a bargain :)

So an enemy you can not kill in a battle where you have to kill all enemies. That is GAME-ENDING. And not only can you not kill this glitched enemy, if it attacks one of your friendly units the game will crash, so both Game-ENDING and Game-Crashing. So if this issue was fixed I might consider re-reviewing the game. If you consider this game for its Tactics game-play get Wargroove instead. If you consider this game for its adult content get another game with better quality art and better game play.

input_text: Great RM title that suffers from some grammar issues but has a solid core and decent story. Includes a free soundtrack, too! Aside from some minor translation errors (improper use of words and spelling mistakes) that are common with most RPG Maker games, this is actually a solid, well-built title. The amount of scripts used in the game (IYKYK) seems daunting, as the more you add to an RM game the more it tends to mess things up, but things gel and work cohesively very well. I've encountered only mild slow-down issues (the game suddenly drops to 5-10FPS) with the Dev having stated they are working on fixing it. A crude workaround is to hit Alt+Enter to make it switch between windowed and fullscreen or vice-versa As for the story, it's actually intriguing. The aforementioned typos are a little off-putting, but it is well crafted and has kept my attention so far. The puzzles are standard, with only one giving me serious pause until I figured out the trick. Then, it was actually rather ingenious in how simply it actually was. Is it worth the price? I got it on sale for around 5 bucks CAD, but I would say it's well worth the full price, and a must-buy on sale if you're a fan of games of this type. For an RM game it has a surprising amount of polish. Also of note: the launcher they included with the game and the extras. I LOVE THEM. It's something I think ALL RM games could benefit from, as it lets you decide if you want to start the game in fullscreen or windowed, and what ratio to make the game screen. It also offers direct links to where they are on your drive (no digging around) to the artbook AND it comes with a full soundtrack which was not mentioned on the Store Page. Bonus!

input_text: My Goddess's Deck Has No Pathetic Cards Story There isn't much of a story here. Basically, your protagonist, Fatima, is the guardian priestess of a nation, Donerksela, and she must help them manage their resources in order to expand their population and increase her power. Sadly, we don't really get much more dialogue than that. Some of the choices can let you be more lenient when it comes to your citizens' workload, but that's about it. We also never learn what's up with the enemies that show up, but the last guardian apparently failed to defeat them. All we know is that once the final boss is defeated on week 90, your protagonist is able to become a goddess or maybe something worse depending on your alignment. Your alignment stat determines what your character will look like, but I have no idea if going for negative alignment significantly changes the story. It probably doesn't change much, since there's no cutscene for winning the game. Personally, I'd like to see how ascending to goddesshood affects Fatima's relationship with her citizens. Gameplay As implied by the above section, the game is all about the resource management and card gameplay. You get a randomized board to build facilities on, and each tile has a preset type of facility you are allowed to build, but some cards allow you to override that restriction. Each facility also has durability that you have to look out for, though at high levels, you might not have to worry about that durability outside of friendly fire with your offensive cards. You generate a certain amount of resources each week depending on your facilities, so try to strike a balance so that you have every resource you need. However, to ensure you can't do a ton of stuff in one week, you have a set amount of EP that gets refilled each week. But what exactly are you spending resources on? Food is spent to increase your population, wood is spent to increase your population cap, gold is spent on passives in the study menu, fuel is spent on repairs and manipulating your hand of cards, and ore is spent on facility upgrades. Passive skills in the study require almost all types of resources, and the nodes you can upgrade are randomized, though you can spend more resources to change a node to something else. Enemies can inflict debuffs on you to slow down your resource production and they will also take up tiles on the map. Worse yet, they can attack your population, causing a game over if your population is wiped out. Because of this, you may want to store up some offensive cards while lowering the enemy spawn rate in the study menu. However, you still need some enemies to show up if you want to farm money for the shop. As for the bosses, which appear every 30 weeks, they have a lot of HP, clear all your resources, and deal massive population damage, but if you win, you get to pick a powerful relic to add a strong passive for the rest of the run. You can gain EXP and manipulate your alignment score to evolve Fatima into her next form. I'm not sure how this affects gameplay outside of aesthetics though. I think some transformations increase the number of card slots, which can help with stockpiling offensive cards. Evolution also unlocks the game animation speed setting in the options menu, but it feels wrong to hide such a feature behind game progress. Verdict 7/10 Once you get a hang of the mechanics, a casual run is fairly well-balanced, though the beginning of the game will be the hardest due to your lack of EP and card slots. Towards the end, you should have so many resources and passive buffs that you actually will feel like a goddess. Unfortunately, the game doesn't have much of a story and the translation is terrible, which makes it harder to learn from the tutorials and in-game manual. Maybe this would be better as a phone game considering how the gameplay loop works.

input_text: Since I am unable to post reviews per dlc because it shows I didn't "buy" the dlc, I'll have to update my review for each DLC that comes out. DLC1: Combat engineer is really cool. It's nice being able to plop 6 turrets down and hold an area on your own almost. The campaign is horrible. 2nd mission in, I am fighting multiple mechs and a vehicle at once. Another time the enemy plops down a reaper turret that kills me in seconds. And this is in the beginning. Absolutely hating the campaign. So far, not worth the price. Definitely do not buy for the campaign, it basically gives everything to your enemy and kicks you in the nuts with it. DLC2: Psychics. Kind of a cool class with different powers. Telekinesis is not nearly as cool as it sounds, since you literally need cars and barrels in order to do damage, and the damage is not as much as some other classes' powers. So it is situational and not very strong. For the campaign: Unlike DLC1, you don't start off with a lot to work with. You begin with an extremely crappy class with barely any skills or slots to put them in. The first mission might as well of been called "Welcome to Dark Souls", and the 2nd mission literally threw multiple Hunters at me. With the super crappy beginning class. I did some save scumming and running like crazy to get past a few missions and can't seem to unlock anything good, so it has been even less fun than DLC1. DLC3: Weapon modding. I'm not sure it totally works for this kind of game, but it is cool none the less. There appears to be quite a few options, but there are not a lot of feasible ones; many options appear to be for niche builds. I do recommend getting this DLC if only to change the bullets of your main gun, so that it is more easy to cover armor pierce or energy stun. I've yet to do the campaign for this one, but until I update for that, just assume it is as bad as the other two or worse since that is the growing trend here. Overall: Each one adds something substantial to skirmish or multiplayer, but the campaigns are by far worse than the original.

input_text: Another great puzzle coming from Sweety Cute Studio. Dances and Girls could just as well be named “Idol Girls” because they are all cast in a singing on colorfully lit stage environment. (Of course, except for the first 10 images the girls are not dressed much like you are likely to see in an idol performance!) There are 10 girls with 4 levels of dress. The first 10 puzzles are quite easy, the next two sets of 10 are generally easy, and the last 10 puzzles are perhaps medium hard, but mostly just take more time because they have more pieces. With my puzzle-solving talent (or lack thereof), it took me a little over an hour and a half to complete them all. The game ran perfectly for me—no crashes, problems changing settings, and so on. input_text: Buildings! Short, medium, and tall. One moment, your lance is leisurely crossing a street with no enemies in sight or even in radar contact. The next moment, enemy 'Mechs are firing atop or behind buildings! I think that in one particular mission, the enemy commander was even singing to me -- "Why do 'Mechs suddenly appear, every time you are near....cause just like me, they long to be, blasting you." But that was not all. That commander was likely laughing as I repeatedly missed hitting one of his lance mates that was firing from atop a building. However, I had the last laugh. All my missed shots hit the building instead. It collapsed (yes, the buildings can be destroyed!). So down went the unlucky 'Mech. The fall damage destroyed one leg and seriously damaged the other. But since excess leg damage transfer to a shoulder, there was damage there too. To add insult to injury, I destroyed the building in front of the enemy Catapult that was firing non-stop. So I was the one singing later, along that beach drinking song's tune (no shirt, no shoes, no problem song) -- "No building, no cover, no problem!" So here are the pros and cons of this DLC, based on the above and other experiences I have so far: Pros-- - new biome (urban city) - some new 'Mechs - some new equipment - if price is a non-issue, this DLC is fun even at full price Cons-- - for many, probably not worth the full price, so just wait until it goes on sale - really the urban setting is the best part of this DLC, with the destructible buildings and being able to expand your tactics because of it - some environmental effects could have been added, like the sound of traffic and stuff - understandable but not quite realistic that the hustle and bustle of the city suddenly totally stops just because your team went stomping in, with some passing civilian vehicle or two possibly enhancing the experience of possible civilians being in harm's way In conclusion: - this DLC is worth getting - the urban setting biome alone is worth it since it is quite the departure from lonely biomes in the standard game - though not realistic, it is understandable why the city suddenly feels like it is frozen in time, since the software developers made all buildings destructible and any additional detail would likely have slowed the game

input_text: Review date: 5/4/22 (Early Access) I really, really, really want to give this game a good review. I do. I just can't do it. YET. My recommendation is to wait until this gets fleshed out a bit more. It's VERY early access, but has a LOT of potential. Unlike some other dragon games I've seen, this one is quite playable. It's just not ready yet. Good stuff about this game: You are a DRAGON! The dragon you play is absolutely adorable. I enjoyed playing this character. You can indeed FLY! Breath weapon is DEVASTATING (as it should be ;) ). Relatively bug-free (nothing that prevented playing, or caused issues playing at least). Graphics are nice, if dark. Now, the bad stuff: Flight burns stamina. Your stamina drains fast, and refills slow. Forget about flying all over and doing devastating air strikes. You don't have the stamina to fly very far at all. Nor can you swim: you basically run across the bottom of the water. Whoops (that's probably just an EA issue). Add to that: melee attacks use stamina. One melee strike uses up almost 70% of your stamina. In other words, you can strike ONCE. OR fly. Forget about flying in and striking. In fact, forget about using melee at all, as one strike didn't kill the first creatures you fight (your breath weapon does, and recharges fast, so it's really your only weapon choice). Melee and stamina need to be tweaked (unless there are possible upgrades later, which I didn't see). If I am blowing through almost all my stamina with one swing, there better not be anything left in front of me afterwards! But there is, so it's kinda balanced wrong. The only way to STOP flying is to fly into the ground (which is kinda clumsy), or run out of stamina (which happens pretty quickly, actually). There should be a button to drop out of flight. If there is one, I didn't find it--it's not the obvious choice of the same button that start flight. The game scenery has all been dark. Not sure if that's the theme the are going for, but having some brighter colors/areas (in town, no less) would be better. I completed the first quest, and am told to return to the quest giver. I have no clue where he is, nor a marker to find him. Wasting a lot of time running around looking for him. There were markers for the bad guys, where's my quest marker to go back? The game says you can cast spells, however, none of those keybinds are working--I tried, when I discovered the hard way how bad the melee attack was--they should be hotkeys 1-5 (or something like that). Nothing happened with any of those. Or they also use the perpetually-drained stamina. However, it's possible I haven't unlocked them yet, as I only did one quest. I may have more feedback as I play more (assuming I ever find that questgiver). I would really love to see a few updates to this, and change my review. For now though... I recommend waiting and see where it develops.

input_text: I LOVE FISTI-FLUFFS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! It's such a cute game, I love all of the cats and their cute little cat sounds. It's easy to tell which cat you are playing as, even when the stages get a little chaotic, and the ability to give them little outfits and glasses just makes them more endearing. I probably like the destruction mode the best, but kibble defense is also pretty high up there and gets pretty challenging the longer you play! There are a few different game modes, all of which are pretty basic and easy to pick up (especially for someone like me that tends to have to relearn all the buttons each time I jump back into a game). If you like cats, silliness, and chaos, I highly recommend this game! The stages are really unique and I love trying to get the powerups for my cats! Some modes definitely feel a bit harder than others, but I think that helps the game feel balanced as you can't win any specific game mode effortlessly. The game is still fun even when I am not "good" at a game mode, it doesn't feel disheartening or frustrating at all. I like getting the unlockable items even though I tend to gravitate back to the same ones each time regardless of which cat I am playing as (lol). The $20 cost might seem steep at first, but honestly I think it's a no-brainer kind of investment. The game has so much going for it, and I am happy to support the developers for basically the same price as a pizza. tldr: Fisti-Fluffs rules! It's not a perfect game but it's got heart and (most importantly) cute kitties. In short, I love it.

input_text: TL;DR: the negative experiences people have with this locomotive are likely due to a lack of clarity in the manual, which I explain in the review. For the price that I paid, I'd say this DLC is a good addition to your collection (actual review begins below). I've noticed that many of the negative reviews for this locomotive seem to focus on one of two things: not being able to move or poor steaming quality. What needs to be remembered is that this is a Pro Range locomotive, and it simulates operating procedures much more realistically than most other Train Simulator locomotives. A large portion of the locomotives in this simulator have the braking functions operated entirely by one set of controls; that is, the train brake lever (the lever on the right in the F4 HUD). However, the Manor (and most other Pro Range locomotives) rely on both the main train brake lever as well as the small ejector to have the brakes function properly. This is why the locomotive won't move for some people; after putting the train brake lever in the release position, you also have to turn the small ejector on ("J" key by default). Once you do this, the brakes will release successfully. Interestingly, the steaming problems that reviewers mention is also caused by misusing the small ejector. In order to create a vaccum to release the brakes, the small ejector uses a lot of steam. When stationary or running light at low speeds, this isn't much of an issue as the locomotive's steam production can usually keep up with this usage. However, once you begin pulling a train at speed, your boiler pressure will drop fast. This is because you have to turn off the small ejector (also the "J" key as it's a toggle control) once you're moving at about 5-10mph. Don't worry, the brakes will remain released after turning it off. Other things that will help boost steam production are opening the dampers (holding the "M" key by default) and closing the cylinder cocks after leaving them open for a few seconds after starting ("C" key by default). Normally, this would likely be an issue of not reading the manual, especially with the Pro Range DLC as most of the ones that I've bought cover this aspect of operation. The thing is, none of this is mentioned anywhere in the manual for this DLC (with the exception of the key controls, of course), which I personally think is a major issue. This is especially the case for someone who's new to the Pro Range and not familiar with these realistic operating procedures. If it weren't for this major oversight, I'm sure this DLC wouldn't have gotten such a negative reception. If there's anything that should be fixed on this locomotive, it's the inclusion of this vital operating aspect in the manual besides a simple keyboard control. As for the DLC itself, I find it to be a decent addition to one's collection. Not the best, but certainly far from the worst. The controls are definitely more advanced than your typical Train Simulator locomotive, and I recommend that anyone driving this (or any Pro Range locomotive, for that matter) use the F5 HUD. The inclusion of Mk. 1 coaches is always nice, and though I haven't finished all of them yet, the two scenarios I've done so far have worked just fine and were enjoyable. However, it definitely looks a bit dated. As someone else mentioned, this actual addon was created by JustTrains in 2013 and was likely re-released under the Pro Range in 2020. The locomotive's appearance definitely shows its age; it was probably good at the time, but it simply doesn't hold a candle to the much higher-fidelity models produced for Train Simulator these days. On top of that, I must also agree with other reviewers on the physics: for a Pro Range locomotive, they're not great. They're better than most standard locomotives in the simulator, but they fall short in terms of realism compared to other Pro Range locomotives I've driven. Additionally, some of the controls are simplified compared to their real life counterparts (e.g. the injectors require no adjustment whatsoever to get water into the boiler, they function more like on/off switches). So where does this DLC sit, exactly? Personally, disregarding the issue with the manual, I think it serves as a good introduction to the Pro Range for someone who may be new to it. This DLC allows someone to experience the more advanced control schemes offered by the Pro Range without the added factor of hyper-realistic physics (which may be seen as a positive or negative depending on who you ask). Would I recommend this DLC? Well, that depends. First of all, I would never buy this for its full price (though I'd say the same about almost every other Train Simulator DLC pack, so take that with a grain of salt). However, for the sale price of $11.99 (what I paid), it's a different story. If you're someone like me whose equally content driving Pro Range engines with realistic physics as well as standard locomotives with basic physics, I'd say this DLC is worth it. For $12 you get a decent quality (but somewhat dated) locomotive in a few liveries, some coaches, and four standard scenarios for the S&DJR. Not the best deal in the world, but certainly not a bad one in my opinion. If you're someone whose new to the Pro Range, I'd still recommend it. It's a great way to get used to the more advanced controls without having to go all-in with hyper-realistic physics (though I do believe that some Pro Range locomotives allow for simplified physics, so this may be a moot point). Just make sure you remember the details about the small ejector I mentioned above (read the manual, too)! However, if you're someone who’s only looking for top-notch, highly detailed, and hyper-realistic DLC, then you should probably look elsewhere. Overall, for $11.99, I'd recommend it, but not as strongly as some of the other DLC packs available for Train Simulator.

input_text: I remember playing the first R-Type Final, developing the OF line, wishing they would eventually get a powerful Wave Cannon. That dream is finally realized, albeit in the form of paid DLC. I wouldn't buy this at full price, but I paid 4.19 USD and I feel like I got my money's worth. First, you get a ship with Standard Wave Cannon III and the ability to switch to a few other Standard Wave Cannons, the "OF Force -" and the capability to switch to any of the other OF series' Forces, and a Purple Pod that fires two shots at about 30 degree angles which can be switched out for other colored Pods in the OF series. The Purple Pod also launches out a bit when you press the Force Detach button. Second, you get free resources in the shop--they'll be listed with the name MARIKO, which will help you develop other cool ships, especially early on. Lastly, you get a pilot helmet and suit that increases the amount of resources you gain a bit, albeit at the cost of a reduction in Pilot Points. Getting this DLC seems to make the entire rest of the OF line obsolete, so combined with the ship itself, the resources in the in-game store, the resources obtained from the suit, and allowing you to put off the OF fighter line until you're doing it to unlock every ship, you're getting some value with this DLC. The ship itself is also very good for beginners who are struggling with the antiquated ships they give you at the start of the game, and since you need to beat levels for resources, this might be a good early pickup for beginners as well. Although, I would suggest trying out the free DLC "April Fool's Prototype" first and seeing if you can get through the game in that. Overpriced, get on sale, good for beginners, actually a pretty cool ship.

input_text: This is a good puzzle game with a very strange story. If you prefer casual puzzle games (like me) over hardcore puzzle games, don't be put off by the comments! It's really not as hard as they're making it sound. There is one part where everyone, myself included, gets stuck (the first statue puzzle in the sewers), but it's not the difficulty of the puzzle that's hard, it's figuring out where the sequence begins. Once you know that, it's just another average puzzle. All the other puzzles just require simple logic or solving fairly easy riddles. The music in the Ghost Coast section is very nice. I really enjoyed that. I also really appreciate the speed at which you can speed walk. You're able to run from one place to the next rather than slowly plodding along. In a couple areas where you need to cover a little distance, this is extremely useful. So this is definitely a fantasy puzzle game rather than a walking simulator. I also love that, even though the game has been out for a couple years, the dev is still actively involved in answering questions, responding to comments, and is thinking about adding a patch to the game. He's also very friendly. Everything works as it should, and there are no bugs, which is fantastic. I'm quite pleased with this game. It's relatively short (only 4 levels), but there are two different endings. The puzzles are hard enough to make you feel satisfied when you solve them, but they're not so hard that you want to quit... unless you're that one other reviewer who rage quit lol. It's fun, and really, that's all you can ask for from a game.

input_text: Edge of War is a tactical, turn-based, (medium) fantasy CRPG. Though, currently there is very little story and little in the way of character development outside of stat and skill choices. All of these are within expectations of a standard issue isometric CRPG. Classics like Persuasion, Stealth and Lore skills currently find very little use, though. The main focus for the current build is combat. The only exception would be Mechanics (lockpicking), which is essential to get the best possible loot. And there is plenty to be found! The setting is somewhat unique among CRPGs as it is apparently based on Finnish folk lore. You will still fight bandits and wolfs. But you will also learn, that Skyrim's trolls are a far cry, of what a troll can truly be. A 10m rock-skinned behemoth, whose scream alone can induce fear into your characters. In the background, and surely part of a narrative to come, is what appears to be an ancient, way more advanced civilization than the current medieval-ish one. Spirit energy (vaeki), a form of usable magic for your characters, based constructs will likely appear eventually, think robot soldiers. Part of one of your missions is to inspect parts of such a construct. I am very hopeful for more here! Noteworthy also are the 2 races that accompany the humans: Hirwio (moose headed humanoids) and Peyko (a mix between an ugly witch and a goblin, still human sized), both of which specialize, where humans are generalists. This is important as you are not supposed to be able to max out everything. Overall it's a bit of a fresh wind, though not too out there. The by far most interesting part about this game is the partial procedural generation of the world. I believe this is a great innovation and improvement on any not too narrative focused RPG. It allows for slight but relevant changes to every playthrough: other enemies, different loot, other special characters, other quest locations, other shops. I am currently on my 4th playthrough and can say that each felt significantly differentiated from the others. On full release this system alone will give this game an insane amount of replay value! As implemented as it is now, I would already view it as a tool worth revisiting for any CRPG developer. For example Pathfinder WotR with this kind system in place might have hooked me way beyond 500 hours (200 hours currently). I believe it is that essential! Lastly, there is the current technical state of the game: It is suprisingly stable and works almost without issues! There are some minor bugs and annoyances to be expected from early access. None of which were substantial or couldn't be remedied with a quick load. Autosave is already implemented and works perfectly fine! I suffered 1 single crash. The developers, a team currently mostly privately developing the game, is also aware of most of these bugs and answers regularly on Steam discussions. There is also a discord for further discussions. Overall I can recommend the game wholeheartedly, even if it's relativley short (per playthrough) at this point. This may just be a true diamond in the rough. I have high hopes for further developments!

input_text: Platformer game from Hentai Room. Does it deserve the negative rating it has? As a magic practitioner, Sofiya, you venture into dungeons and cemetaries to discover the history behind your clan's rules. As you progress through the 45 dungeons, you will find books revealing bits of the story, but don't expect much here; the explanations are vague and way too brief. There is only one ending, and you can rather easily find all of the books, so one playthrough is sufficient to see everything. The focus was placed on the platforming parts. Ok, I get it. The moving pace feels very sluggish in comparison to similar titles, but it is not as detrimental to the gameplay as other reviews describe it. I won't count it as negative. It is what it is, and I got used to it shortly after starting. Aside from platforming, you also have various enemies to deal with. You have only one basic attack and three special ones to fight them. There is not much variety here, even considering that it is a budget title. After a few hits, most enemies will wave a white flag for a moment. You can then activate the sex finisher to eliminate them. This takes a few seconds and can't be skipped, so the pace suffers. However, with the double jump, you can avoid most enemies, so you don't need to kill them all. Especially since you don't gain experience from fighting, just recovery items and special shots. The main difficulty of this game is the platforming aspect. Most spikes are one hit k.o., and there are no checkpoints, but the levels are very short, so I don't feel like checkpoints are necessary in the first place. I certainly did not struggle much to complete levels, and I managed to clear most without any deaths. It is not a precision platformer, so I don't get why people cry about the difficulty. I'm certainly not a pro at platforming. Similarly, the three boss fights are pretty basic and easy to win. Next, I need to mention some negatives. Despite being a short, budget title, the lack of creativity is evident. There is very little variety of enemies, levels feel samey, and there is no character progression. Even at this low price, I expected a bit more. I can't say I hated playing it, but I was not very amused either. To the developer's defence, I believe it is the first platformer game he has made, so perfection is not expected. Still, more could've been done. I rate the experience as neutral. The pixel art is somewhat below average. The finisher animations lack polish and quality but are fluid enough to see what is happening. Sadly, there is little variety of scenes. Dungeons lack creativity as well. Some are way too short, and others feel too bland. Certainly, more work could be put into their creation. The visuals are slightly below my expectations as well. The music is pretty simple but mostly fits the theme. Nothing really stands out, but nothing sounded annoying either. Just good enough. The sound effects are a bit lacking, though. No bugs encountered, but on one of the levels, I fell on spikes that did not kill me. Rather insignificant glitch. Overall, a very simplistic platformer with some sexy pixel art and okay music. Even for a budget title, it all feels a bit uninspired and repetitive. I find it hard to recommend this game, but my actual rating would be neutral. It's certainly not the worst I've seen, but more effort should've been put into the development. 4.6/10

input_text: My Experience I'm often drawn to stealth games, especially when I'm given clear information on what enemies can perceive. Although it's clearly a budget title, the trailer and screenshots for Heist Master led me to believe that it could provide this type of information. And honestly, it does - it's clear when you're in an enemy view cone (the cone turns red), how far the sound travels when you step on a metal floor or shatter glass, and when you're hidden by smoke and can remain safe from enemies or automated turrets. Your thief can dispatch enemies quickly with attacks from behind, and can don costumes that allow him to traverse certain areas without detection (for a limited period of time - these costumes seem to disintegrate after a period of time for some reason). I was generally able to complete the levels quickly, especially when the four-digit passcodes and keys are so clearly visible in the game's isometric perspective. Within each set of levels you can purchase upgrades from time to time to enhance your thief or reduce the effectiveness of enemies or cameras in the levels that remain in the set. I would usually purchase some of these (I didn't know what else to do with my money), but I wouldn't call them necessary for success. Although the game was cheap, I still found myself wanting more cohesive and substantial content from it. I played sets of levels in a variety of locations (the casino that you see in the trailer has nine levels), and it felt as though these levels were randomly pulled from a bag. As I played, both locations and levels seemed to be repeated. After a while, I found myself just trying to unlock all of the characters, since the game provided me with no larger-scale goal. The last character I could unlock was Spider-man, but unlocking him required completing randomized sets of challenges. One of these challenges was using a zipline a certain number of times. It was easy to use ziplines, since your thief is essentially required to use them for basic traversal in various levels. However, the game seemed to be randomly pulling together levels that included no ziplines, so I was unable to complete this challenge. This was the final blow for me in terms of spending more time with the game. Heist Master is generally bug-free and is solid mechanically, but really seems more like a demo than a full game. I'd be interested to see developer SoupInIt Games put together a game using these mechanics that actually has a story or an arc to it.

input_text: First, I want to point out that a lot of people are complaining about poor translation. I have played the game thoroughly and, for the most part, it is properly translated. It starts to get iffy toward the end but it's bearable. I think many players may be confusing translation with 1st and 3rd person writing. In this game, it switches between both and the only indication is the lack of a name for the speaker. This applies to Irell as well as the Princesses so it can get confusing rather quickly. The writting format is pretty basic but enough to get descriptions and thoughts across. There's a heavy focus on how Irell Reis feels about every little thing. Some dialogue gets repeated despite already encountering it based on who you are following, ect. Probably about half of the dialogue boxes should be merged together or removed entirely to reduce redunancy. The game would do a lot better overall just by enhancing the dialogue to make it more relevant. It would also be more believable and immersive if the vocabulary wasn't juvenile and overused; ex: "cute", "plebian" and nobility titles. I would like to see the game revised this way in the future, or have their next game written more eloquently. Some of the voices sound like they were recorded at a low quality. Personally, I listen to the first few lines of a character and then turn it off. Most of them sound identical aside from tone. I enjoy imagining their voices on my own, with or without the tone implied by the creator. It's very difficult to know who you've picked to follow or how to continue to properly follow them without a lot of trial-and-error, unless you use one of the player made guides. There's a few on Steam that work well. I recommend using the Story Line portions first. After that, you can replay the game to get any of the Achievements missed. Holding the space bar down will rush through all of the dialogue. It should only take a few minutes to get them this way so definitely enjoy the story line first. Most of what you read is based on original lore and backstory for the characters. Once you've triggered an ending there is a -lot- of reading. You will need to get every ending to learn every characters story as only a few interact per play through. Also, keep in mind that not all of the character stories are updated at the same time. Each ending varies in length. One of them was a good 3 hours of reading after the choices ran out. I didn't expect this as it was my first playthrough so it quickly became a case of "when is this going to end?" for 2 of those 3 hours. If you like plot twists, and the ones in this game can get ridiculous, as well as learning about characters then it will keep you playing until the end. Fair warning, it gets ridiculous. The artwork, for some of the characters, was very well done. I would have liked to have seen more stills of events, especially during major scenes and Dyanna's finale. It would have made the bloated dialogue more bearable and the story more immersive overall. The UI needs some work. All of the options in the menu takes a little bit longer than normal to load and usually feels like the game hasn't registered the request. By the time I move the mouse over and click the option a second time it loads. The Quick Save & Quick Load options are not explained. You can only manually save or load during dialogue where it is listed to the right. [Having now completed the game, I will say that overall it has a low quality plotline from character to character. Personality preference will determine how much you enjoy the game. If you get bored with a character, I recommend either holding space bar and finishing to get the achievements or drop them entirely and move on to someone else.] It's worth it at 50% off, plus free DLC. 6.5/10 could be a potential 8/10 as a VN with polishing I recommended.

input_text: This is a game about being away from your family for work. A parallel commentary from the in game character and the Game Designer. (One of the Game Designer's family plays the family of the protagonist in game) I beat the game in right about 5 hours. No crashes or glitches. My wife watched me play and she and I both really felt the emotional impact moments from the game. I thought there were spots for some achievements, but maybe not many. The game starts out as a straightforward mystery, and then takes a turn to the surreal. This is more of a game to inspire contemplation rather than wrap everything up nicely. Most of the progression on the mystery is done via optional objectives, and if you don't do them you will be totally lost at the end. If you do all of the optional objectives the message of the game is deceptively easy to understand and only obfuscated by the preconceptions that you bring. Good game. Surreal ending, but good game.

input_text: When I saw the videos and description of Ravenmark, I thought I had stumbled on another hidden gem like Valkyria Chronicles. Alas, there are not much hidden gems and most times you will just pick up another little pebble. Ravenmark is such a disapointment that looked good at first glance. A warning should have been the fact that Ravenmark is an iOS port. While that doesn't mean that it automatically has to be a bad game, there are still some implications that come along with it. Games for portable devices almost always don't want to bother the player with decisions that he made in earlier stages of the game. Concerning an RPG or strategy game, this effectively means that there are most likely no player choices to be made like specialising the skills of your units, upgrade units after a battle and carry it over to the next or RPG-choices that affect the course of the story. In short, you can expect that everything that adds salt and pepper to a RPG or strategy game will be left out. This, sadly, is the case with Ravenmark. The following list rates the different aspects of the game using a scale from very bad (---) to very good (+++): Stability/Bugs: +++ No bugs or stability issues encountered. Good job. RPG-aspects: - The story is a railroad slideshow without any interaction or possibility to make choices by the player. The characters are flat and either unmotivated good, bad and/or naive. Sometimes there's a voice narration of the character's conversations, which is nice. Tactical aspects: + You can give direct commands only to a maximum of six units during any given turn, while you will have at most times more than six units of yours on the battlefield. You can group units together and these new formations can be commanded with only a single command. Unfortunately, formations will often times not do or will not be able to do what you've ordered them to. All in all the tactical aspects are okay and the formation system adds a nice new idea to the genre. Strategic-aspects: --- There are simply no strategic decisions to be made. You can't upgrade units or characters, you can't decide which units to bring into battle, you can't decide on which terrain to fight, you have no choices regarding infrastructure, unit supply, economics or whatsoever. Price: - Considering the fact, that this is an iOS port, 15 € comes pretty close to a rip-off. With the lack of RPG-decisions and no strategic value, Ravenmark comes down to a casual game with some boring slideshow story. Honestly said, I wouldn't want to pay money for that no matter the cost.

input_text: I enjoyed the game far more than I thought I would. Though i'd really call it more of a visual novel than a game, but the gameplay and choices are already better than most visual novel games out there in my opinion. In this game, YOU are the Sleeper, you are expected to self-insert. Make the choices YOU would make, consequences be damned, but above all, survive. Something about this game and how it played, and how it was written, and choices it allowed you to make just kept me hooked. The hours played (at this time, 12) reflects one entire playthrough of both the base game + free DLC. And I enjoyed every bit of it. The first few "cycles" as they are called in this game, can be brutal if you don't prepare for it. Once you get past the rather oppressive early game (which is very thematically fitting and would not have as much impact on the game if it were not there), this game carries itself extremely well. However, It doesn't take much for your character to go from barely surviving, to thriving, and being incredibly resource rich. While this is also fitting in a way, it also kinda detracts from the experience a bit, as halfway through the game, I pretty much stopped worrying about every experiencing a "game over" and stopped worrying about my "condition". However, by the time I became "overpowered", the story had me hooked, and I was already happily on my way to finish the story and decide my fate. I got this game on sale and it was more than worth it. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a fair bit of reading in an engaging way, and with a game that makes your choices matter, encouraging you to press on.

input_text: So I will give the game a very minor recommendation. The games graphics are quite good; the organs look good however I wish there was more detail. The environments look good but I felt were underutilized. Excellent voice acting, I really felt all the actors were putting effort into their roles. Whether it was the disinterested security guard or the main character, trying to maintain his professional composure while clearly harboring some deep mental problems. I will try give my observations of the game while avoiding spoilers. This game has potential but it fumbles what could be something very interesting. The medical language used in the game clearly shows the devs did their homework on this on the nature and process of preforming an autopsy. The bodies in the story I felt were well designed, however that ends when going to autopsy only mode. The observations are all randomized but they use the same male and female models every time, which is a shame because I know the devs know how to make detailed models but those are only in the story. the story is also quite linear with virtually no deviations. I will admit the secret ending surprised me but it wasn't exactly shocking and I got it without even knowing that it was the secret ending. The game's story is short, you can finish it in one sitting with no problems. Technically it runs fine, never crashed on me and there weren't any glitches [that I could find]. However, some of the minigames were a bit frustrating; it requires precise movements and when cutting certain things, if you are even one pixel off then it won't register complete. In the end, I feel if this were a longer game with more story and character development then I feel like it would be much better and I believe the autopsy only mode is a missed opportunity with how they designed it. So I would not recommend this game at full price but I don't think this is a bad game per say, a good foundation but with not enough content to take advantage of it. I don't know the full intentions of the devs but I feel like if they had more time with this game before releasing it they could have made a much better game. So while I like it, I can completely understand why others don't. TLDR: Not a bad game but wait for a sale.

input_text: I recommend the game but please read the long review. In this game leveling up is easy. But quite grindy to maintain that upped level properly. This is a really cute game AND equally tough to manage lol.. 😂 I request to DEVs please don't get me wrong. The game is honestly cute. I love all characters walking around, lively city, shops to buy ingredients, the graphics style, recent HUGE and FREE bakery update, Just because of this cuteness and my love for cooking games made me buy it even though I knew I'll never be good at this game. 😅 This game is solely for multiplayer. Solo players like me will look for a moment to breathe if gone wrong. Customer patience meter is low and food servings available in one cook is low as well. So when your restaurant is gaining fame, customers will come in more. Each of them won't have much patience, the food servings will end in a blink. But before you can cook the next serving -- your customer will rush out in anger. 😡 There's no setting available to turn up the patience meter longer or increase the servings number. So a solo player is never able to offer more than 2/3 recipes in their restaurant menu .🙄 The cooking process is not very easy as well. You'll level up soon but you gonna need couple practice cooks to offer servings after servings to your customers without loosing them. Ingredients will run out quickly. Every ingredient needs extra step to be prepared to use in the cooking/garnishing which is realistic I'd say. It's very easy to make mistakes during cooking if you're not paying attention. And throwing away food will decrease your ingredients quickly. In the middle of rush hour -- you'll find you're out of ingredients. You gotta wash your plates too or you will run out of plates to serve customers. Another and again another hurdle! 😭 Don't worry. There are some perks you can unlock to mildly help yourself, not much though. There's a Free mode too but it's a little odd. It's not like you're able to run a restaurant in free mode. It's rather a practice mode, NOT a sandbox mode. It's unnecessary but I use it to memorize recipes I've unlocked in career mode. So that I can cook and offer them to customers quickly. 😮‍💨 The game isn't much graphics heavy which is good. A mid-range PC/gaming laptop can handle it. The DEVs have recently released a whole free DLC to introduce baking side of culinary and a new map. Another con is -- some career mode recipes are locked behind gourmet challenges which I don't like. It's not fair to insist to enter a challenge to unlock recipes. 🙁 The game is addictive but a little simplicity, and a real Free/Sandbox restaurant mode with lots of customisable options are needed. There are some pesky bugs too which enters quickly but takes time to go away.

input_text: A great sequel to Persona 5. Some of the characters who were mostly on the sideline in the original story have new story arcs, *cough cough* Haru, and the story is overall great. The jails in all the different locations are unique and they'er different enough from the palaces to stand out, but some of them are way too short (Kyoto and Okinawa especially). The soundtrack is amazing, some of the jail themes are insanely good (Anti Hero and Counterfeit Phantom are my personal favourites) and the gameplay is really fun. It's about what you'd expect from a Persona hack and slash, all the characters have differing combos, weapons and ways to play them (for example skull can charge his special attacks to make them hit harder and fox is more about throwing a bunch of hits quickly), the thing i personally liked was that every one of joker's personas changes his showtime animation a bit and they also change some of his combos a little. Now the glaring issue with this game, the performance, this game can't handle newer multicore cpus for some reason, you might even experience crashes alongside the ridiculous frame drops, BUT using Process Lasso and setting it to performance mode and giving it usage over all cores, P and E alike, might remedy it. Personally for me after I used it, the performance went back to what I would've expected, no frame drops, always 60 fps and most importantly NO CRASHES! Also the Digital Deluxe edition and 2 DLC packs aren't worth it, you already get enough items from playing the game and the legacy bgm is cool but not worth 10 Euro.

input_text: First impressions: Extremely polished and bug-free for an early access release. The same good ol' D**mRL action. (Let's all take a moment of silence to extend a gigantic middle finger to Bethesda/Zenimax lawyers for going after that wonderful fan project.) But the dungeon changed. I didn't encounter an equivalent of the stairs to Hell's Arena in my run, so I dunno if the dungeon is a reskin and we can expect to encounter familiar places under a new name, or if it's a complete redesign. Redesign is better I guess, to get brand new content to play, since we can still download and play DRL, which is even getting new updates thanks to this game. I know most monsters are simply reskinned from D**mRL with the same mechanics, but I find the new sprites, sound and names well-chosen. Not knowing the capacities of a new, large enemy was really scary again, good job there. Some enemies also have variants (frost, poison) which I don't remember from the predecessor game. Perks have been reworked, for instance Reloader lvl2 is more powerful than lvl1 now, and lvl 3 has the effect from the previously separate "Shottyman" perk that depended on lvl2. One major, welcome convenience is that weapons that drop from enemies are always empty of ammo. Gone is the compulsive alterning between the G (pick up) and U (unload) keys to make sure you loot every bit of ammo on the map to make sure you don't penalize yourself. This is one instance where I'll take gameplay over "realism". If you're coming to this from Jupiter Hell and not D**mRL, prepare to enjoy the various liquid floors (water, acid, lava) and the destructible walls, they add so much to the atmosphere. I have some minor gripes with the UI (such as the one for modding weapons) which takes too many clicks and keystrokes to perform some actions, and makes it hard to compare weapons properly. Also, level generation is sometimes not that great, cutting off sections behind large bodies of acid or lava, which are very expensive to cross, and placing teleporters and levers that are too dangerous to be worth trying. Eventually, you'll figure out ways to deal with it, but those situations will always drain your resources, sometimes for nothing in return. (BTW, if you never experienced the original DRL, it's free, you can download it from chaosforge, or even easier, get the DRL mod for this game from the Steam Workshop.)

input_text: Game idea shortly is to get the key and reach the next level and find collectables while rolling around in a marble that is affected by gravity but depending on level has one or more forms it can take to use abilities that are needed to solve the level. Abilities can be light form, floating form, fire form or metal form. Noteworthy is also that the controllable marble ball is not a flipper ball that gets thrown around helplessly - instead the player has pretty good control over the ball plus ability to execute double or even triple jumps if executed correctly. This results in the player jumping around pretty nimbly from one ledge to another yet evey now and then there are places where you need to do precise jumping - and the control over the marble ball allows the player to do just that. Rest be assured though if hard platformer games are not your tea as on average this game is more casual and based on overall mood rather than a true skill requiring game. Level design is simple but good enough. Mostly ice caves, fire caves etc with switches and collectables. Light is important in every level as you need to be able to see where you are going. Sometimes you need to flick switches to be able to see properly. Soundtrack can be very moody or epic. Certain songs reming me of Two Steps from Hell which is not a bad thing at all. And how does this game compare to some other titles? Marble Mayhem: Fragile Ball it is not. This does not require that much raw skill although certain levels may frustrate younger players. Collisions and Nightsky -games are closer but this game has more control and does not get as frustrating. but may loose on better level design and challenge if that is what you want.
